div.head: LADIES' LETTEIL,
div.p: LADIES' LETTEIL,

Dran NELLIE, So far as the new summer gowns are concerned there are two shades which are certain to achieve tirlarity. The one is a delicate fraise or straw-. tint, but more akin to the artistic old-rose tone than to the true strawberry shade. The other is a dainty mauve, which suggests a pale Parma violet, but has a bluish tone. The tailor is using a dood deal of brown, which will be worn later on, but grey is the tint for spring, and when summer comes it will be discarded for brighter hues. Sashes will, it is said, reappear with muslin gowns, and painted ribbons, or those of fancy chene and flowered design, are to be worn over plain muslin. For my own part, Ido not expect this fashion to be very popular, but soft chiffon and mousseline de soie arranged as a waist scarf, and tied at the front or side, is more harmonious with the closely-fitted skirt. The princess gown is invariably completed by a bolero top of some description, and even the corselet skirt, with its fall blouse, is not considered chic without a bolero of the abbreviated type. The straight-fronted corset is responsible for the long-waisted effect in front of blouses and bodices, and even the belts are arranged in some species of point to give length to the figure. It is quite certain that there will be no great change in the fashion of skirts.

Dainty headgear is always acceptable, and I have seen some beautiful examples of late. For instance, one of white-Cuba straw was especially Petal, verf fine and light, with underbrim of tucked chiffon, and two small rosettes of hydran- gea-maave silk, while the upp :m trimming consisted of taro large choux of silk, one mauve and one ivory, and a garland of tiny long-stalked mauve and white flowers, delightfully natural-looking. Another pretty bat of natural Tuscan straw had a wide wavy brim, with black roses and green kliegs nestling under it, and above big ehoux of ivory and palest green silk, and another rose. Hats of the sunburnt type are to be fashionable, and many modistes are already displaying burnt steams, with the huge black bows of which we had such a surfeit last season. This may be popadar, and not fashionable, but the burnt straw, with black tulle and roses of several tints intermixed, is a charming complement to a black gown. A

delightful hat of burnt Tuscan straw, with double brim, is ere now disporting itself in the Sunny South, and is certain to be a model to be repeated for many clients. Its trimming consists of a deep mauve tulle, much tucked, and forraing a raised loop over the left side, where it is joined by a graceful tuft of heliotrope, which wanders in a thick wreath all round the right side of the hat. Under the brim is a cluster of tila.a velvet bows, collected under a fancy buckle of steel and pasta. Domestic dyeing is invariably a failure, no matter how excellent the formula of the dyeing material employed, and the net result is generally the making of a prodigious mess, and the spoiling of the garment after an outlay in time and money for materials approaching what it would have cost to dye the garment properly by sending it to an expert. Certain small articles of female attire, such as ribbons, silks, &c., can be dyed with a fair measure of success by means of prepared dyes sold by chemists and oilmen; but when it comes to dyeing a garment like a livery coat, it is much better to send it to the dye-works. If it is worth doing at all it is worth doing properl,

As to blouses and slips there are any number of the prettiest. In one exaniple black and white satin fauhril is the material, the front being finely tucked, and the yoke, collar band and cuffs being of transparent lace. A silk slip might be utilised to wear underneath a charming affair of rose-pink silk, with the many tiny tucks of the yoke so arranged as to give a check pattern ; while then a broad shaped insertion of ivory lace. simulates a bolero effect, and beneath this long lines of tuck. hold in the fulness to the waist. Your loving

WINDOW CORD& —When windows are difficult to open or close rub the cords with soft soap, when they will run smoothly. A SILK CLEASSER.—To cleanse grease from wool or silk, Apply a fluid made by dissolving 2 oz. white soap and oz. borax in one quart warm soft water. Pour a small quantity into a bowl, add the same amount of water, and sponge the material with it. After it is clean, sponge with clear water and hang it up to dry.

The Duke of Cambridge was looking ve,y seed when be opened the Military Exhibition .at Earl's ent,rt the other day. This perhaps can hardly b., wool ,ed at seeing that his Royal Highness was born in 1819, aril that he has .always lived a busy and strenuous fife. The Dukedom will expire with him, owing to his morganatic marriage wi h Mis, F.-irc. brother, who was a burlesque actress of note in hr.*d.v. The rnatfh,ve took place in Dublin, where the Duko was retying with his regiment. His only surviving sister, the gratin Duchess of Mecklenburg-Strelitz is three years younger than himself. _

She was the wife of the late Mr W E Gladstone's elder t,rother, s r Thomas Gladstone, who died tweice years ago. Tile Gladstonen of Fascicle House were always strong Conservatives, and when Mr W E Gladstone tcod for Oxford ['Myer/0(v, his brother Sir Thomas, voted agait..t him. D spire however, the strong political difference,tt between F4-cifie House, ar.d Ellswarden Castle, the la e Lady GI tdstnee wagon the most friendly terms with her brothei-iritlaw, and his wife, the late Mr and Mrs W E Ci!aristone, et Havrarden.

The general vlew of thi,e yeae's Exhibition at the Royal Academy, is, that on the whole, it is a disappoin- I ting one. Those who go to see the pictures and not the dresses only, will scarcely find a canvas that will live in the memory. The place of henour is, of course, given to M Benjamin Constant's portrait Nf the late Q..ierie, which, draped in black, hangs alone, in erlendid isola- tion. at one end of the principal room. Tie was where Mr Orchardson's portrait group of the Boyal Family hung last year, which also was overpraised, and suff,red by the contrast in its failure to come up to expac,•ation• So it is with the Benjamin Constant por•rait oh (111.P11 Victoria. It coaveys but a feeble idea of t he personality of a great Sovereign, and in its failure to reproduce any ctrikiag impression of the royal presence, it leaves one with a sense of disappointment that the artist has not made the most of so great an opportunity. As was t Case last 3 ear, M. Sargant furnishes the principal attractions of the main gallery, with hi, por- trait groups, the most strking of a,hich, on the present eccasion is the " Dasighters of A. Wertheimer E q." Ths absence of say striking features in this year's Auademy leaves M. Sergeant easily first among the exhibitors. It is comparatively easy to tell the great artist's work by the striking way in which his figures grand out, as sleasat in the solid flesh,lithough am a rule, pessibly, these portraits are of more Interest to the artist tnan to 'the public generally. Most people turn to the subj -ct pictures for that which interests them most, and here again they will find Burlington cuse very dis, ppoint- lag. There are not any more war pictures than usu.', though one weuld have thought that these wi u'd have been a special feature. Altogether there are some tws or three hundred fewer canvasses than last year, but this, undoubtedly, is act a disadvantage. Those of us pessessed of a craving for novelties in table decoration, will find the following Japanrsque scheme decidedly effective. For the fl,wers, provide nowise ofl Imrai or Kegs ware, three parts filled with damp sand, Over these spread expanded paper fans, the spokes on the bowls, the paper e xtending beyond them. Take neat little sprays of flowers, wire them and drive tham in between the sticks cf the fans.taking c ire that the stems of the flowers are pushQd well down into the sand, which is to keep them fresh. The SiZ 39 of bowls and fans must be guided by the numbers needed, and by the SiZ3 of the table. One tiny arrangement for each pair of guests, and half a dczen large bowls (all ut six to eight inches across) will probably prove sufficient. In spring fruit blossoms, daffodils, and narcissus or iris,are s ppro; r at,. Summer brings on embarras de rickesse, and autumn oars afer us sprigs of pine quite appropriate for ourpurpose. flowers are preferable to elinabere and , As a rule one fan is enoogh in each bowl, but two or three penny one, ears be grouped together on a stand large enough to hold them. There is much to be said for the new fashion in society for the pairing at guests at dinner partiee. Everyone knows the awkward pause in the drawing room, Er+ say nothing el the whispering and speculation that goes on beforehand, as to who is likely to he one's partner at table. Much of this is now obviated by the handing of a card or note to each gentlemen with the request "Will you take so and so in to dinner." This In a measure, anticipates a some awkward ceremonial and greatly simplifies the departure .for.. the dining ream. Four or five years ago, each sleeve of an up-to-date bodice wail larger and fuller than the bodice itself, last year saw sleeves of an equally extravagant tightnees, at the present time a happier state of affairs obtains for a medium allowance of apace is bsiog granted us. Sleeves will remain fairly closely-fitting at the top, and some will merely be slashed and puffed at elbow and cuff. The newest sleeve of all however, comes not far below the elbow, where it ends in eitagg, rated fulness, either drawn in puff-fashion, or allowed to flow out in a hell. This shortness will be met by lacc,muslin, or silk under- sleeve., or merely by long lace gloves or mittens, Apart from the coolness of these sleeves, there is the very de- cided advantage of the possibility of constant change and variety, as the undersleeves, like the gloves and mittens, are moveable and interchangeable with other bodices. Many an old bracelet lying half-forgotten in its case, will be brought out to suit this new style, serpent—like armbands with many coils, being of good service in clasping the sops of long gloves closely to the arm. In washing ehirts, linen and cotton accessories save much trouble. Thread lace is an old friend, and there

is a feeling now for the white trimmings, both for the frilling and lor the open work (woven) embroicery, that in form, r times was considered suitable for undergar. mt ors only. Mrdern patterns are very elaborate aud ffectivr, and the work is Satiifaetory, especially to those who can forget the associations that connect it h night dr sees and underwear. For shirts and for lingerie, the new washing ribbons are just the thing. fhey supply an often desired touch of co'our, and moreover are warranted to withstand the illusage of the laundress. Millinery is certainly cheaper thln rf yore. It is still possible to eon heavy prices for Paris models, and to pay for costly plumes and first rate fl -iwers, the price that they are well worth, but, for ordinary occasions. clever fingers ar d a moderate sum can be made to pre. (lace most satisfactory results. The ready-made bat- mounts,ranging in price from 2s 11A.1 to a guinea, or even more, save much trouble, as, when well chosen, they merely need,at most, rearrangement to fit them to ' the incividual. Expert workers can of course buy and use the raw materials, but the time taken in making these up renders the saving scarcely worth effecting. With the still lingering s.ilor or " boater," two or three larger shapes,and a stock of interchangeable mounts, or trimmings, the average girl is set up ia millinery for the season, while for packing,the movable bows and plumes save much space. Much good millinery is put together merely with pins (as tilts° save fingering the mat.-rials) and are invisible, or else show pretty ornamental heads' Stuffed Eggs.—Cut some hard boiled eggs in halves, mix each yolk with a teaspoonful of grated cheese and a small piece of butter. Season with salt, cayenne and a grating of nutmeg. Refill the whites and serve on a bed of cress.

div.p: A SPRING TRIBUTE

A stately tomb! anent where spring's bilis shyly peep. Wherein nut Empres.-Queen MD3413 tisleep. A sweet oblivion of rat, wbile dro,ping willows weep. And loyal subjects kneel, in Lfflictiors sad and deep.

Our bereavement is sore to boar, our rerced eorercign called ' To realms of Queens and Kings, throne of our Heaven- ly Lord, Europe and the universe mourn in solemn accord— No more kind messages from her—no sympathetic word. Spring weeps for her Deity, none in the world so great, Whose sway was hailed supreme in every state-- An absolute autograph, used wisely and temperate, With gentleness, charity,—yet firmly and so sedate. Beloy'd by the human race, for she shared their cares, Her soul, I fluence, wealth, and love wore their's— In spring, summer, autumn, and winter, for 63 on years. She was their friend and Queen—departing 'midst a nation's tears.
WILLIAM FIAMP6ON,
Whittingham. Preston, Lancashire, May, 1901.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, MAY 10, 1.901
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, MAY 10, 1.901

He learnt, too, that they were ill-paid and open to bribery; that the prison 'discipline, which was theirs to enforce, tended to brutalise the warder at east as much, if not more than, the prisoner over thorn he tyrannised • and that, with the prison Minence and surroundings sapping the human and iigher instincts out of him he was open to be note easily influenced by those who knew how to )lay upon the weakest and worst side of his nature. It did not take him long to discover that whilst he prisoner's effort and aim in life was to deceive he. warder, it, was the warder's aim to play eye- ervant to the governor and deputy. To get a ight lagging was to earn it by screening the warder 'rom the deputy. Oftentimes did the deputy make i surprise visit, and though half-a-dozen warders lye minutes previously might be indulging in lelinquencies, yet from one lag to the other the word would be passed along, and finally to the warders, so that it was the rarest thing for a varder to be caught in the tot of relaxing •egulations. The lag, too, who could discover a case of )ribery, as the burly companion -of Martin had 'one, was sure to do a light lagging. The warder in charge of Martin's gang, the man who had killed ;he mouse and felled its owner to the floor, had rice received a large sum for smuggling in tobacco o a rich convict. The burly prisoner, Hawkins, iuring one of his spells of freedom, had discovered this, and was now making good use of his knowledge. • . _ .

He hd once suffered the cat, 1.00 for fighting mother warder, and since then the officer had been thoroughly cowed and always kept out of his path. Another efficer, who had been in the struggle and had cut Hawkins's eye open M the fight, had suddenly been killed two months afterwards. A pure accident., so the jury found it, for a lump of rock had fallen on the warder's head during some excavations. But the staff of warders knew that Hawkins had been on the top of the quarry when the stone fell, and they all stood in fear of him. Hawkins, feeling sure of his position, played his minis well. He was cringeing and subservient to the -governor and the deputy. He played the repentant sinner to the chaplain and was accounted the most promising case in the gaol, notwith- standing the fact that he had been playing the same wt for two previous Lerma'. The warders would have subscribed five pounds apiece to have given him a chance of escape, knowing fall well that they would have an opportunity of firing a shot which should rid them of a dangerous enemy. But Hawkins was by no means over anxious to give them the chance.

div.p: ( CopzlngV.l
THE LADDER OF GUILT.
BY ITLYSS ROGERS,
Author of "For Love and the Queen," "Wedded in Mystery," &c.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: Douglas Low, madly in love with Grace Hendon, daughter of a neighbeuring farmer, attempts to murder his cousin, Martin Fenwick. His aim, however, un- accountably fails, and Squire Fenwick, his uncle, is the victim instead. ,The deed was witnessed by an old hag who has a grudge against the Fenwicks, and who accuses Martin of the murder. Martin is tried and found guilty. The execution fails, and a second attempt a week later is also abortive. Martin Fenwick is reprieved, and removed to a convict prison. Meanwhile, Douglas Low meditates new villainies. At his prompting Farmer Ilendon's granaries are fired.
CIIAPTER X. LIFE AT MINEWOOD.

It was nearly dark when at length Minewood was reached after a weary ride and a tramp from the village station of Langleigh. The grey walls of the prison, overhung by a heavy mist, rose up in sombre, surly welcome, and there was the sniff of the brine coming up over the rugged upland which somehow spoke to them of wild freedom and boundless liberty. It gave them renewed hope, and was a thousand times better than the depressing climate, the leaden air of Henlea.

A meal of bread and skilly was provided after each man had been ushered into his cell, and presently Martin was ordered out again and marched with the rest of the new gang, and some from another prison, before the deputy-governor and the chief warder. Here the records were examined, and each man was identified. Thence they were•marched into the presence of the prison doctor, who commanded that they should be stripped, and inspected them one by one. There were more objects than one in this pro- cedure. Not only was the doctor able to satisfy himself as to the health of the convict, and the chief warder, who had followed into the doctor's room, to compare any body marks by which the prisoner had been and would be through all his penal career specially identified, but by this means no convict had the slightest chance of .smuggling anything into the prison. Martin was stripped ready for examination, and was shivering& waiting for his turn after a tall, heavy-jawed man, whose back was scored with deep, red cat-slashes that told their own tale, when a startled cry from the rear made him suddenly turn. He was justin time to see a convict strike a warder to the floor with his Set. The next instant the man, half-stripped, was felled by a truncheon to the earth, where he lay insensible. "What's the meaning of that ? " said the chief warder fromlhe other end of the room. The warder who had been struck advanced to the

doctor's table....ll;bela-e-o-ineifiTri-g-i-n.Ti:i;and: "I found the prisoner smuggling this into the gaol, and ,I took it out of his pocket and killed it. Then he suddenly struck me." He flung the object, for which the convict had risked the severest penalties, down upon the table. It was a tiny, grey field-mouse, quite dead. The warder's fingers had throttled it. How the man had succeeded in bringing the field-mouse with him was beyond conjecture. Martin learnt afterwards that the man was a new "lag," and did not know the ropes, or he would have been aware it was impossible to get past the doctor's searching examination and not be d,tected in the possession of his little companion. It had been his friend through six long weary months of silent probation, and had cheered the darkness and monotony of the cell during many a miserable hour.

"I could have borne to have parted with him, sir," he said,,, when called before the deputy- gov,ernor, "but when the warder choked him before my eyes I couldn't hold myself in, sir. I'm very sorry.! • But his sorrow did not spare him. The laws of a convict penal establishment are as inexorable as the laws of nature. But the thought of his inno- cent little companion in misfortune who had met such a sudden end helped him to bear his two dozen lashes with the cat bravely. Martin little knew at the time how this incident would affect him. But at the moment his whole soul went out in sympathy towards the man who had resented the killing of the tiny pet.
Martin was a keen lover of anfinitls. Here was

a fellow-prisoner with whom he felt he could make friends. A man could not be wholly bad who could attract and tame such it playmate. Ile resolved to keep his eyes open, and when the animal-loving convict had served his special sentence, to, establish a friendship as far as was possible. The next morning the prison was astir at five. It was barely light, but the, summons of the bell had to be obeyed. In accordance with custom, a warder presented himself at Martin's door and inquired if he were well. More often the query was couched in negative form. "You don't want to see the doctor, I suppose? Nothing wrong with yer, eh ? " After this greeting came breakfast, the usual skilly and bread, then cell-cleaning, chapel, and ' work, the men parading before departing in gangs to different parts of the settlement, and each being searched.

Martin having almost regained his customary strength was marked for heavy labour, and accordingly he fonnd:himaelf Marching out of the prison gates with a gang in the charge of warders, each having drawn.truncheons, whilst a suggestive hint as to the impossibility of escape had pre- ceded the prisoners. in the shape of armed sentries, with rifles loaded and bayonets fixed ready for any emergency. These men had; taken up their positions at various points of vantage, and formed a cordon all. around the seat of operations. Any man who made a dash for liberty had to run the gauntlet of passing the rifle of one or other of the sentries. It was montonous work that which was assigned to Martin. With several other men he was deputed to build a boundary wall. Huge boulders of stone had to be brought a considerable distance for this purpose, and Martin was told off to assist a big, heavy-jawed convict in carrying out this duty. "'Ere," said the big man, "you do the wheelin'." Martin looked up it the warder, only just above them, expecting to see him descend in wrath upon the man for daring to speak aloud and give instruc- tions, but the warder did not seem to be taking any notice. Picking up the barrow and leaving the rest of the gang Martin proceeded to the place where the stones joy, a hundred,and forty yards away. • "Look 'ere," said the burly convict. "You're a new lag, a gentleman lag, ain't yer ?" "I hardly know what you mean said Martin.

“Well, it ain't, no good beatin''about the bush. Don't you give yerself no airs 'ere. The screwe'll be down on ye with 'arf a word from me, don't you make no.mistake.” Martin kooked at the man in great surprise. "I ain't jokin'; I ain't. I've done three turns at this place before, and . they know me, you bet. An' what's more, I know them. It won't do for none of them tO fall out with me, I know too much for 'ein. I could open the governor's eyes, I could. An' that's why them an' me's pals, so to speak." "Then why don't you work it to escape?" "'Tain't good enough. They would just like their chance, they would. They'd put a bullet into me as soon as look, and be glad of the chance to get me out of the way. So they would to Smiley Sam, No. 389 over there, and one or two others; second timers and old lags. An' this place ain't so bad„, after all, when you gets, tkie upper 'and of 'em like I 'ave. Ah, 'ere we are. Now then, you just begin Anil load the barrer." "But aren't you going to help?" • "Not me. Wot do you think? I'm ganger, that's wot I am. You just buckle into it." Martin did, not because he was inclined to do this big work, but because a warder was approaching, and he preferred to be on the safe side and allow his companion to get into trouble by himself if he chose. But the fellow took little notice of the w4rder, merely making a semblance of work for form's sake when the officer was near. Martin -Was wholly amazed. It was possible then, even here, in klinewood prison, with the warder standing over one with truncheon, and the sentry but tt few, yards away, with loaded rifle, to assert one's independence and to defy warders and regulations alike. How was it done? He discovered subsequently, and the discovery led him to more loathing and disgust for prison system and method than all his own privations. He learnt that among the warders it was possible to find men possessed of principles little better than those of the criminal Bock they had to shepherd.

div.head: CHAPTER XL
div.p: CHAPTER XL
TIIE FIGHT WITH BELLY HAWKINS.
"'Ere," said he to Martin one day. "I 'aren't • 'ad any toke from yer yet. You ain't as big as I lobe, so jest fork some over." "Toke ? Do you mean bread?" „ . .
"Of course I Means bread, so don't be so nice- mouthed about it."

"And why should I give you why of my bread ? "Now, don't come to arskin a lot of silly questions, hang yer. I'm a 'ungry man an' wants it more than you." "I shall do nothing of the sort," replied Martin. "Besides, if I wished to do so I don't see how it's possible." "You jest shove it under the door; I'll arrange for the rest," said Hawkins. ."

Martin did not reply. He had no wish to force on a quarrel with this ruffian with whom he was obliged to hold daily intercourse, but, all the same, he did not mean to be terrorised by the man. It puzzled him, too, how Hawkins would manage to get the food if he put it under his cell door. But he discovered afterwards that it had been easily worked in several other cases. There was no other way to account for this except the aid of one of the warders. The next day no sooner had Martin and Hawkins drawn off by themselves than the bullying convict, in a towering rage' approached close to Martin, and, gripping him by the sleeve of his tunic, hissed in his ear :

"No toke this morning. Remember, I've warned yer." Martin was a well-knit fellow, but the man who had threatened him was a veritable giant, a good two inches taller than any other man in the prison, convict or warder. He stood over Martin with his teeth clenched, an expression of diabolical fury in his eyes. He had bullied many a prisoner into acquiescence in his wishes. Old 'lags took care to keep out of his way, and new lags who knew him trembled when they were told off to do duty with him.

The man still continued holding Martin by the arm and glaring at him with his tigerish, eyes. "Leave go," said Martin. "You'll get no toke from me. Take your band from my arm. Don't play the fool, man. You'll get into trouble if the screw sets eyes on you." The man laughed a hideous laugh. "You green- horn. What screw do you think would interfere with me? Not one, not even if I twisted your arm off like this."

His grip tightened on Martin's arm. Personal physical insult of this character in Violation of prison rules he did not feel called- upon to bear. With a clever wrench which somewhat surprised the bigger man he slipped his arm from the other's grasp and stood defiantly before him. "You mealy-faced gentleman lag," snarled Iliwkins. "Don't think you're going to come it over me like that in any such easy fashion. Take that for a start, Jipd- 401.11 let, me 'ave any more complaints to make." He swung•out his powerful arm before Martin had the faintest idea of his intantion and felled him to the ground with a crashing blow. For the moment Martin lay half-stunned, and a dozen convicts rested at their work to witness what would happen next. The warder who was in charge of the gang saw what had happened, but he pre- tended to maintain an interest hi something quits in an opposite direction. It was an unwritten rule that if two prisoners quarrelled and started 'fighting, to let them fight it out unless the chief warder or the deputy-governor happened to be about. In fact, the warders rather enjoyed the fight and they held the opinion, probably a correct one, that if two men had a standing grievance it would be settled more quickly with the fists than any other way. To interfere meant the necessity of reporting, and in the case of Hawkins, Warder Whitaker, who presided over the gang which included Mzirtin and the bully, had no desire to fall foul of the man, who, he was certain, would get the better of any row. Martin lay for a moment; then all the hot indignation in his blood gave him strength. Though slow to be aroused, yet when he was inflamed no regulation could restrain his im- petuosity. He rose to his feet, clenched his flats and, forgetful of warders, of regulations. of every- thing save the insult and the blow, rushed at his persecutor. It is not much to say that Hawkins was a poor judge of character. He was taken completely by surprise, for he had not expected so quiet-looking, so extremely gentlemanly a lag to retaliate. But before he was aware that he had any serious work in hand a.blow between the eyes forced him to stand at once on the defensive. By this time thirty convicts and a couple of warders with a sentry on a distant mound were interested in the fight, and, kept careful watch as the two men settled down to the conflict. Martin followed up his first blow by another on rho; point of Hawkins's jaw, and the bully, maddened by pain, instantly deserted his defensive tactics, and sought to demolish his enemy in one fierce, aggressive rush. _ _

But it was a test of skill against mere physical force. At school Martin had been able to hold his own with any of the gymnastic trainers with the gloves, and he had not forgotten his early training. On the other hand Hawkins, though he had been victor in half a hundred rough-and-tumble fights, bad never yet undertaken a deal with science, and a dumbfounded him to find that after plunging desperately and striking sledge-hammer blows at his lesser and lighter opponent he had produced no other result than to wind himself. He stood back after two minutes of such exercise, panting loudly, whilst Martin, fresh and agile, delivered another blow on the point of the big man's jaw. Driven to maddening desperation Hawkins again plunged violently into the fray. His blows would have felled an ox, delivered as they were with all the concentrated hate of his evil nature. But the supreme difficulty he found was in getting them home.
Bully Hawkins, as be was known at Minewood, ttad met his match at last. Blow after blow did Martin deliver, well-timed, accurately-aimed blows, which accomplished the work they were intended to do.

There was breathless silence among the onlooking Jonricts and the two warders as the battle pro- , gressed. At the first no one doubted the issue, but when it seemed likely that Martin would prove the victor there were none so gratified as the officers, who hated Hawkins whilst they truckled to his sullen outbursts and blinded tlaeir eyes to his frequent omissions of duty.

Hawkins was rapidly going under to the incase sant, vigorous, and well-timed attacks of his oppo- nent. He was wholly on the defensive now, tough once or twice he indulged in a blind mil and sought to sweep his enemy from his nth by sheer brute strength. At length he could mad to the attack no longer, but adopted a ruse which would only have suggested itself to a vile, unprincipled ruffian lacking all honour, such as he. Suddenly backing to a heap of stones which it was their duty to remove he called out at the top of his voice! "Help Help!" But no warder took any notice. They were too delighted with the thought of his thrashing. He was still yelling cowardly when Martin sprang at him, and with one final blow knocked him sprawling in the dirt.

"Havewyou had enough ? " cried Martin, stand- ing over him. "If so get up and shake hands. I don't want to be bad friends, but I won't be bullied by you." The bully raised his head from the ground and looked round, but not a warder was taking the slightest notice apparently. With a bad grace, therefore, he rose to a sitting posture and held out his hand. Martin took it and grasped it, but little did he guess that the show of friendship was but a mask for the deeper and more venomous hatred this man bore within.
From that day forth Bully Hawkins preserved a grepsy deference towards Martin, but in his heart he 'nursed a terrible revenge, which only waited its Opportunity for fulfilment.
CHAPTER XII. THE VOICE OF THE TEMPTER.

The perpetrator of the arson at Fenwick Barton had not been discovered, though Farmer Hendon, assisted by the police, prosecuted every inquiry. Douglas Low pretended to offer his unremitting services, which were more often pointed in the direction of throwing dust in the eyes of the detec- tives. Not that he had any great desire to be instrumental in keeping Zeke Parr out of gaol. It would have been a Matter of extreme- thankfulness to have seen him committed for twenty years. But the Parrs held his fatal secret, and he was bound. At times so harassed was he by this thought that he would half make up his mind to brave their woid. No judge, he argued, would give counte- nance to the tale of an old gipsy woman who had sworn first that she saw one man commit the murderous deed and then, scarcely a year later, came before the tribunal swearing against another'. But if the - judge failed to believe her, Grace Hendon - would not, the people of Fenwick would not. There had already been ugly speculations as to why the Parrs had been so specially favoured at the Chase recently. Whence had old mother Parr got her cottage Whence came the money that Zeke Parr was so freely spending about the village These were pothouse and backyard problems, discussed quietly, but with animation nevertheless.

A week after the fire Douglas Low sat in the chimney corner of old Barton kitchen. Opposite sat the farmer. There was no light save the 'flickering glow from the hearth. Grace had gone into the village. They were unlikely to be disturbed. "I am glad you called," said the old farmer, slowly, "for I should have come over to the Chase to-morrow if you had not. It's this fire, I find, that's done it. I can't possibly meet my creditors. I looked to my wheat, sir, to clear the interest for the year and to help me a good hundred and fifty pounds towards wiping off some of the principal as well. And now—', _ _
The old man could proceed no further. His head fell forward and he gazed hopelessly into the fire. _ _

"I know," said Low. "You are troubled and wish to consult me about the ground rent. Well, never mind about that. It can stand over until next year. I shall not be lacking id my duty as trustee to my cousin's property in making that arrangement. It is what he would have wished himself."

"Aye, that he would," said the old man. "lir. Low, I'm much obliged to you. But even with that help, there seems to be no prospect of my carrying on the farm. It will have to go. Four and thirty years, sir, have I been here, and worked hard to clear the place, and leave something for my child. :And now, just as I thought I should begin to get my neck from the yoke, this comes upon me. It's very hard, sir, very hard." "But there's a way out of the difficulty," said Low.
_ "What way " questioned the old man, eagerly. "Borrow."
"in-cleink myself more deeply in debt ? " "Yes, for a time. Another good year and you may perhaps retrieve _your fortune. There is another way, but I—" "And that is—"

"Persuade your • daughter to marry me. But I do not press that way, added Low. "I would not urge her against any feeling of sentiment she may still retain for somebody else." "Nor I," said the old man, quickly. "Though that'will die off in time. I can wait my time. Mr. Hendon." "If," said the old man, and-• Low saw that his evil seed had found its way into the soil, "if. that were so, if Grace could see that way, I should welcome it." r. "I am but a poor man at present," said Low; „"merely a steward, but a steward of that which is bound to come to me sooner or later. Had my uncle known, doubtless the will had been different. But as it its the Chase sadly needs a mistress, and there is enough and to spare even at the steward's table. In the event of my marrying Grace I should not hesitate to make myself personally responsible for-the Barton. You understand? "

understand; I understand, sir," said the old man. "But will you pardon me saying that it must be all of her own free will. I would rather starve, sir, and she with me, than force her into a marriage against her own liking." "Of course; of course," said Low. "I don't think there would be any difficulty were it not for this old infatuation. It is possible that that could be shaken off. A word from you," he added, rising to go, "might do much in that direction. I think you gather my meaning." Farmer Hendon did gather his meaning. And he knew that if he wished to save the farm :and preserve his own integrity in the eyes of his creditors he must do it at the sacrifice of his daughter, which he would not do. Nevertheless, when she came in later in the evening he thought no harm could possibly result in sounding the ave ~W nt hl. I w depths of her attachment to Martin Fenwick. He approached the matter gently. "You h to-morrow mft needs e dMs a Martin yet, t, yiy darling?"inofa'ae heard from before a letter is due. You know he said that he should be allowed to write a month after leaving the gaol at Henlea, and if he left exactly at the end of nine months, as he said, he must have been in his new quarters three weeks. Oh, what a dreadful age it seems. I thought perhaps they would have taken him to Minewood, and every day I ran out as the trains from Henlea passed and watched and waited at the railway gate. I thought if he were going past he would be sure to look out at the old farm and then he would see me at the gate. But I never saw him. They must have taken him to one of the other prisons." "I see, my darling," said the old man, throwing his arm around his daughter's waist. "He is as much to you as ever? " . "Father," she said in some surprise, "what a question for you of all people to ask I You know that nothing could ever make me foiget Martin. Neither distance nor prison walls could in any way affect our love for each other."

"You still believe him innocent? " "More than ever I did. There is something seeps assuring me that some day things will be made clear and Martin will beset free. But why do you ask these, questions just now ? " "Never mind, my darling," he began, but A woman's instinct prompted her to say in inter- ruption: "Has Mr. Douglas Low been here?" _

yes." "Father," a sudden shade of pallor crossed her features, "father, he has not--1" "Hush, my child. Ask no more questions. Have no fear. Mr. Low did make a foolish request, an impossible request of me, but—" "It was quite impossible?" "Quite. I see it now more than I did then. Kiss me, child, and go to bed." "Let the worst come, whatever it may be, she shall.not be sacrificed," he said to himself as she left the room and went upstairs. Sleep came tardily to Grace's eyelids that night. A sense of impending danger haunted her, a danger she could not define. And when she awoke after a troff.L.Ad, dreamy night, the same stranger sensation of fear was the dominant impression, (To be continued.)

In 1899 an Order was made constituting the riparian auttiorities of Manellester, Salford, and Stret- ford the Port Sanitary Authority tor the port of Man- chester. fhe expenses of executing the Order had to be borne in the following proportions :-11anenester 4-9;ns, Salford 49 hs, Stretford 1-9th. Tact Order expired on the3l.st Mareh,lB99, but had bleu continued by further Orders of the Local Government Board. In August, 1899, it was proposed by an order of the Board to eon- sticute a P ,rt Sanitary Authority of all urn au and rural districts abutting on the Manchester Ship Canal and the River Mersey, and by that o der to give each authority separate representation and to require riparian authori- ties to cent ribute towards the expense At the inquiry Mr Alderman Walton Smith, the ehairman of the Reelth ' Committee of the city of M anchea-e , stated that he was instructeci t o ask for an order by the Local Goi-ru,nui Board on the lines that Mancheater anould ciav f - nintns,Salford four-einths and S retford one-ninth; sub- ject to this that if any infectious disease on board ship that went to any other port down on the S lip Canal the:authority of that port should he responsible for those infectious cases being taken to the hospital." He stated that the estimated expensee of the Port Sanitary Authority for that rear were £635. Warrington agreed to the propose I arrangement, &nu were prepared to deal with any Case of infectious disease brought . into the town in its own hospital. Ai Order was thereupon pre- pared by the B .ard in accordance therewith, but it would appear that strong objectiOn was Matsu by severaj of the riparian authorities to it. In July, 1903 the Corporation were invited to express their opinion on a resolution wiled by the Manchester Port Sanitary Authority, on toe 18i June, 1900. In reply to that invitation, the Town Clerk wrots to the Secretary of the Local G lvernment Board on 7te August last,that !Awn saw no objeeeion to such permanent Order being made as requested by the Port Sanitary Authority,but pointing out tnat the observations which the Town Council desired to make upon the latter part of the resolution were that the basis of contribution would be unfair to some autboaties if charged upon ratable values, and that in their opinion the ITIDSC equitable method of levy- ing the espouses was that proposed in the draft Order recently issued by the Board. The Town Council would, however, have no objection to contributing to the expenses pro rata to the tonnage of sea-going vessels bound to and discharging goods within each district. Owing to the action of twe or three of those authorities who obj.ctei to the resolution proposed—although he thought they saw now they bad rr.ade a mistake in opposing it—they were asked to attend the local inquiry which was held at Manchester on the 12:h April. The latest proposals of the Board were clic,: Salford and Stretford should have independent represent :Men, but the other authorities should only be represented by one member appointed by the Urban and District C.aineils of the district. Warrington was to send one represeata- tive appninted by the Town Council and Rural District Council jointly, but for various reasons, expressed by the Mayor at that inquiry, such as the difficulty of con- stituting a Joint Committee to appoint a representative for Warrington and the Rural District Council, the unfairness of having to contribute as proposed 1-13th part of the whole expenses of the Port Sanitary Authority considering that few if any vessels ever stopped at Warrington, and the difficulty of apportion- ing mill exponses between the two C et 3., they objected to agree to such an order being made as now proposed. All the other authorities present except Mane chester, Salford, and Roneorn expressed their determi. nation to oppose the Order, and to contest it in Parlia- ment, but he was told for all that the Board had consen- ted to grant the Order and it would, therefore, be for them to see what st,.ps shou!d be taken in cenjunctiou with the other riparian authorities to prevent the Order becoming law. At a meeting on the 29th April it was resolved that the superintendent and six members of the brigade be allowed to attend the annual demonstration of the Lan- cashire Fire Brigades Friendly Society to be held at Rochdale on June Bth, and that the usual allowance be made for expenses, and that the brigade be provided with proper appliances for opening sealed hydrants on private premises in case of fire. Councillor SMPTIIIIRST prooosed the confirmation of the minutes and Councillor PLIMPTON seconded. Councillor lansfox asked for an explanation of the resolutim that the brigade ho provided with proper appliances for opening sealed hydrants on private premises in case of fire. Councillor &SETIF:MST explained that the matter arose through a visit to the works of Messrs Fletcher, Russell and Co, who had fire appliances on their own premises. There were a number oi sealed hydrants on this private property and the brigade had no power to break the , seals or cut the wire, until they got the permission of the water committee. In case of fire it was necessary that there should be immediate access to these sealed hydrants. There were other hydrants which the fireman would use thstriftelves in the event of a fire.

• --Tile —minutes were—re-oiled. Success of the Electric Lighting Undertaking. Further Extensions Aftreed Upon.

Mr Fiume attendei a meeting et the Tramways Corn- mutesad submitted a report on the subject of the pro- posed extensions of the electric lightinatetion, a sum- mary of which was givenia our last issue. Toe com- mittee red o nmended : "That an application tis Envie to the Land G wernment Bird fee their satiation to the borrowing of the further sum et £15,030 for extensions in accordance wite ths above report!' Alderman Musks inevel toe cnnfiren aloe of the nairiums, and in atiu ling to P. resolution that the Sae-. veyor obtain escim aces for pitching the river bank in front of the electric lighting station, said that was a matter that might be left over for toe present. It would come before the cementtee again. With reference to , electrin meter rentsme did not think that any discuesion was likely to arise over them. They were the usual charge's, and the setae propesed Was a fairly average one, as ascertained from what Was being charg.:d in other towns. With regard to the proposed expenditure of about £15,000 in electric li4tring, it had been prac- tically forced upon the committee by reason of the success of the undertaltiog. (Hear, hear.) Is would, he thought. be useful to put before the Council certain figures to satisfy them asito the eanecess which had been so far obtained. !There wes evidently al, desire on the part of consumers to take the light freely. and the anticipa- times of the committee bad been realised to the full. Thb total receipts for the quarter ended, 31st March amounterl to e 1157 45 d, and the expenditure to £417 is 91, so that on the revenue aecount, as it was celled, tiaere was a slight halaece of kill 2s 4d to the credit. In addition to that teere had been a certain ante) tot of expenditure in con- nection with the lighting of tne street lame, but as it was not intended to charge the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee until April let they had no credit brought into the account, or that would have been so much more to the good. Altogether, the ace mint would show, on working expenses account, a balance to the credit of £lOO. (Hear, hear.) That Was not, of course sufficient to clear all expenses, beeetree the capital out- lay had been large and the beak interear and com- mission and sinking fund amounted to £1149 6i 61, so that they had that sum to carry forward to the present year's account. Considering the circuinstances under which the committee had carried on the work during the quarter when they only bad two or three customers at the commencement and the majority only towards the end of thi quarter, a consumption of 21,000 units might be considered fairly satisfactory, and WAS sufficient to justify the committee to make preparation for the increased demands which would be made upon them next winter. (Hear, hear.) He had received a return from Mr Grimsdale, the electrical engineer, which showed that no fewer than 8,607 8-candle power lamps had been actually connected, that applications had been made equal to 857 more, and they knew ot a further 639 lamps which were to be put on as soen as arrangements could be completed for the porpos.; so that they would have not less than 10,103 6-can 11e power lamps within the next month or two. Other people were favourably considering the expediency of using the light, and there was every probability that by ri,xt winter they would have an increaae of another 5,000 lamps at least. In the report origitally submitted by Mr Preece he made an estimate as to the probable income and expenditure and his estimate was based upon 10,000 8-eandle power lamps. The Council would see that they were already supplying a quantity in excess of what Mr Preece made in his estimate. (Heatehear.) The matter had been made more urgent to some extent by reason of tile proposed actioe on the part of the Tramways Committee. The Electric Lighting Committee had to be ready to supply the current to drive the tramcars when the lines were completed, and the present plant did not give any re- serve power beyond the lighting of the town and the driving of the tramcars. That was why his committee had come forward that night with the proposed further extensions. It should be understood that there was) no extension of the building in any way. When the original proposals were before the Counciethe buildings were erected to accommodate more plant than was then required, and the present extensions only showed the wisdom of the proposals as submitted at that time. It was difficult to imagine all the questions that might be out to him and, therefore, he ceuld not say more, but the committee were unanimous in these proposals, and they had only aereed to bring them forward at the urgent request of Mr Preece, the consulting engineer, who had had considerable ekperience in these matters, and he assured the committee most certainly that if they did not go forward in the way proposed they would, in all probability, find themselves in meta P. difileulty as the Menchester Corporation were in at the present time in having cus- tomers who had to wait six months before thy could be supplied with the eleatrie current. The suctiess of the station depended upon the committee being able to supply all the light and power that was asked for, and it was a work of such a character that they could not afferd to be behind with it. He did not say they were at all too previous. He thought they had come forward at the right time, and he hoped the Council would see their way to epprove of the proposals. There were two firms in the town who had under consideration the advisability of taking the current for power purposes. One was a Much larger firm than the other, and at present they were not agreed as to the terms, but he thought there was a chance they would come to terms. They had several other applications for the power, which was en much to the goed and in excess of the 10,000 candle-power lamps to which he had referred. (Hear, bear.) Alderman Feracronen secondel, and the minuttes were agreed to.
The Corporation Tramways. Tenders Accepted
THE EXAMINER, FRI DAY, MAY IQ, 1901

div.head: Councillor Bennett and the Aesthetic Side of
div.p: Councillor Bennett and the Aesthetic Side of
the Question. The Warrington and Northwich Light Rail-
way.

Tramways Committee recommended that the tender of Mr J A Ewart for the construction of the permanent way at £28,739 be accepted, subject to a reduction of time for the executioa of the works, the approval of the Engineers of the quality of the sets to be used, and to the sanction of the Board of Trade to the borrowing of the money; also that the tender of R W Blackwell & Co. Ltd., for overhead equipment at £4,833,191 Clio posts and brackets to be according to design No 1) be accepted, subject to the approval of the Board of Trade to the borrowing of the money. A letter from the Board of Trade was read at the meet- ing of the Tramways Committee approving provision- ally of the system of electric traction proposed to be adopted under the Warrington Tram way s Ord r. At a meeting of the committee on April 30th. the Town Clerk reported that be had received from the solicitors for the Warrington and Northwieh Light Railway Order a copy of the order containing the clauses submitted by the Cheshire County Council, and that he had not received any clauses submitted by or agreed to with the Runcorn Rural District Council, the Stockton Heath Parish Council. or the Manchester Ship Canal Company. It was resolved that the Town Clerk give notice to the solicitors for the order that in the absence of definite proposals or agreements with res- pect to the construction of railway N 1 the committee are unable to a4ree to the application for the order. The MAYOR, in moving the adoption of the minutes said the members of the Council had had in their hands for some days the report of Messrs Preen° and Cardew, upon the various systems of construction and traction, and no doubt by this time they were satisfied that the Committee had been well advised in deciding upon the particular system which it was proposed to adopt. He would remind the Council that the question of having electric tramways in Warrington had been thoroughly thrashed out and settled, and an application for power to deal with this important matter had been made and granted. They now came to the practical part of the butiness, and they submitted a resolution proposing the acceptance of tenders. The Committee also submitted minutes referring to the Warrington and Northwich Light Railway Order. The members of the Com- mittee had considered this matter with perhaps as much or eveq more anxiety as they had, considered the question as effecting tramway construc- tion in the horough itself. They had had no previous experience of what might be involved in the proposals of the light railway. Therefore they bad had to be guided step by step by circumstances as thell had arisen. He thought therefore that the final statement which they tad made, subject to the approval of the Council, would commend itself to their judgment. They had agreed with the promoters of the railway that they should have the option of purchasing that portion of it which ran tram the terminus of the Corporation line on the Wilderspool Causeway to Stockton Heath and round to the Swing Bridge at Latchford. Conditions would be submitted later on, but in the meantime he thought it would be sufficient to say tnat the promoters bad agreed with them finally, and the committee consented to support the application and did so on Saturday last before the commissioners appointed to consider the matter. The decision of the Commissioners had not yet been received but it seemed probable that it would be favourable to the granting of the order. Alderman MONKS seconded.

Councillor BENNETT, in referring to thn Corpration tramways, said that in face of what Messrs Preece and Cardew bad afticl, it was impossible to do otherwise than come to the conclusion hat the committee had acted wisely, but he was bound to say that he still did not regard the overhead system as by any means an ideal one, and he thought that their electrical engin- eers would be able to improve upon it in the near future. He proceeded to express his disapproval of the engineers' statement that the objection to the system on &esthetic grounds was not a serious one except in the case of fashionable resorts where the attractions and amenities of the place were the first consideration. Mr Preece had taken that view before the committee on previous occasion and he (the speaker) wished to protest against it in the strongest possible manner. The fact that Warrington was not a beautiful town made it all the more impera- tive that by may means in their power they should

endeavour to consult the aisthetic side of any scheme which they had in view and try to improve the appear- ance of the town. to the case of a beautiful town it was not so vitally important. Attractive towns could stand a certain amount of ugliness without suffering materially, but in a town like Warrington, which was purely commercial and inartistit. it seemed to him that , wherever there was any possibility of considering the ssithetio side they ought to consider it in the most serious manner possible. lie was sure that anyone with eyes in his heal or soul in his b itly could notpretend to say that the overhead wires were anything else bat a disfigurement. He had seen them in certain towns but never without feeling a sense of revulsion. If this was, the best their engineers could .do for them it was a- long way from perfection. He hoped before long an improved method would be adopted. (Hear, hear) Councillor Trustrou asked for an explantion as to what the." design No I of posts and brackets " really was. Couneillor, Bennett had said they did not possess a very beautiful town, but it was just possible at any rate that by a selection of posts of an ornamental and usef ul'deslo they might mitigate the nuisance. He thought the present design of electric lighting pillars was a very happy one but they were too light to carry the wires for the trams. He could see they were going to be in the awkward position of having to pull down these posts and waste a considerable amount of money, or else have two posts side by aide—one for lighting pur- poses and the other to carry the electric tram wires. He did not tlynk this was very desirable and they should, at the outset, have obtained pillars which would support the wires and also-do for lighting purposes. A design of the post and bracket PM produced and the Mayor intimated that an effort would be made to obtain pots to serve the double purposes of supporting th- wires and electric lights. Only a few of the existing pillars would have to be removed. -Alderman Moises said there was no reason why the pillars should not serve both purposes. Only four or -Ave of the existing ones would have to be removed, and they would be ntflised in other streets when the exten- d ins were made. When the present design was se- lected the tramway scheme was so much in the air that it was felt that they could wait for it, especially in view of the fact that the pillars would not be wasted, .

-Alderman SH&W GREEN said he was net going to ' oppose the intoduction of the tramways, far from it. He thought they, ought to have the best means of loco- motion they could obtain. But on the other hand the expenditure would be somewhat of a tax upon them for some time to come. He was informed thit there were the figures somewhere, showing the number of people who travelled by the vesent 'buses, and he should have been better satisfied had such information been supplied in addition to the report. Be was a little bit disconcer- ted when he found that Messrs Preece and Cardew put down £27,000 for the construction of the roadway, although a contract for £29,000 had been ac•epted. It did not look as if their figures would be strictly adhered to. He hoped the Committee would take every oare to see that so far as possible when expenditure was incurred they were getting a good return for the money. He hesitated to agree to the spending of anything that would be a tax upon them, and he hoped that care would be exercised in seeing that no more money was expended than was necessary, and that so far as pos- sible only lines would be laid where there was an antici- pation of reasonable traffic to provide for the expendi- ture incurred in them. The MAYOR said that if they added Messrs Preece and Cardsw'a estimates together they came to £33,000 whereas the two contracts amounted to £33,500, so that was not a bad estimate on their part. In regard to the estimated expenses and revenues the report gave as much information as they could possibly obtain at this stage. Figures had been supplied by liar Longdin with reference to the 'bus traffic on the Liverpool and Knuts- ford roads and the estimates of Messrs Preece and Cardew had been based upon the amount of traffic necessary to make the line pay. The committee had been wisely led to decide only to commence with that portion of the work which was considered would be most likely to pay almost immediately after it was put down. The rninotea were then passed. Sunday Concert Regulations.

The General Purposes Committee recommended that the repreeentatives of the Cmporation on the County Joint Cominittees,or other public bodies be allowed their out-of-pocket expenses when attending meetings. A notice of the intended sale by the Rector of Grappenhall of Gleb3 land in Wash-lane was laid before toe com- mittee. It was resolved that admission to Parr Hall on Sunday evening for sacred concerts be not allowed before 8.15 and that no charge be made for admission to such concerts. The minutes also contain the copy of lettera patent by the King conflrening and renewing commissions of the peace. The MAYOR proposed the confirmation of the mioutes. Tbo DEPUTY-MAYOR seconded, and it was carried. The Lighting of Orford-lane.

Connellfor PEACoes Moved " that the Gas Committee be requested to light the lamps in Orford-lane one hour earlier than at present." He said he bad repeatedly brought this matter before the members of the Council and he had received several complaints atout the streets being in darkness for an hour before the lamps were lighted. There was a great amount of traffic and in the narrower part of the street especially it was very neces- sary that the lamps should ba lighted as early as pos- sible. It was 9.30 on Thursday night before the last lamp in Orford-lane was lighted. This was really too late and he suggested that the lamplighters round should be modified. Councillor F R ROBERTS seconded the motion and re- marked that the easterly side of Orford-lane was in St. John's Ward and he was one of the representatives who were responsible for its good government. If it were true that the gas lamp were only lighted one hour after dark he thought it was something approaching a scandal Of all the highways and thoroughfares that ought to be lighted he thought Orford-lane was the most Important. It was the thoroughfare leading to the Barracks and he thought it was very expedient indeed that light should be thrown upon the doings of the military in that por- tion of the town and he had therefore pleasure in seconding the motion. Councillor SMETHURST and Alderman Hunataisost supported. Councillor JOLLEY, also speaking in support, referred to the advisability of a general re-arrangement of the lighting of the town. He pointed out that in certain parts the lamps were allowed to remain lighted two hours after dawn, while they were not lighted until two hours after sunset. If the committee would mend their ways in that direction great satisfaction would be given to the inhabitants of the town. Councillor TINNION said this matter had had very much conisideration. It was hu.uoht about through hav- ing two aldermen in the chair and vice-chair.(Laughter). The DEPUTY-MAYOR (chairman of the Gas Committee) said the remedy lay with the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee. The Gas annmittee carried out their contract with that committee, which was to light the lamps 3,940 hours per armlets'. to other towns the average nuinber of hours the lamps were lighted was 4,800 It was a question for the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee. Alderman SUTTON said the Gas Commt.tee was paid well for its gas lamps. Alderman straw GREEN said that if there was a divided responsibility between the two committees the question should ha settled before taking a vote. The MAYOR If we pass thia resolution the Gas Com- mittee will report upon it. The proposition was then carried. Compliment to the Deputy Town Clerk. The MAYOR Said that befor, tney separated he would like on their behalf and upon his own to offer hearty ,t congratulation Vs the Deputy Town Clerk who had pass- ed his final law examinatiol. (Hear, hear) 'They had now two lawyers on their staff, and expectd very groat things from them. They all wished that Mr Wilson and his wife and family would enjoy this social promotion, and that for Mr Wilson it would carry its commercial valise for very many years. (Hear. hear.) The Council then rose.

STOCKTON HEATH.
Parochial Committee Meeting.

A meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee was held n the National Schoolroom on Thursday last week. Mr Davenport peesided and there were also present : Messrs G. Pilling, J Clarke, J Whitley, Mason, Pemberton, Fairhurst, Pearson, Knowles, with G F Ashton (clerk), J Farrington (nuisance inspector) and J Swinton (surveyor.)

div.head: ELiCTION OF CHAIRDfAN.
div.p: ELiCTION OF CHAIRDfAN.

Mr Pearson, speaking as the oldest member of the Committee, considered it a privileee to be allowed to propose Mr Charles Davenport as their Chairman again He rejoiced to think that they had retained Mr Daven- port's services for another term as their district coun- cillor. It would have been a distinct loss to Stockton Heath if Mr Davenport had retired from public work. He had given his great experience as a builder and as a public man for a great many years and they had come to look upon his services as invaluable. At any rate that was his (Mr Pearson's) estimate of Mr Davenport's services on the committee.

Mr George Pilling seconded the proposition, and said they could not improve upon Mr Davenport. The proposition was unanimously agreed to. Mr Daymport, in acknowledging the compliment, thanked the Council very sincerely for the renewed con- fidence placed in him. IG had always been his endeavour to give every member of the Committee a fair and reasonable bearing, and he was sure be had always received the greatest courtesy at the hands of the mem- bers. He ought to apologise for irregular attendance at the meetings of the District CouLcil. This was due to ill-health to some extent but more particularly to over-pressure of business. He was happy to say that in consequence of the assistance he now had in his busi- ness he would be able to attend the Rural Council more regularly drying the ensuing three years. He would endeavour to give them every satisfaction as to reason. able attendance. He did not think it was requisite for I him to attend every meeting but when the business made it advisable for him to be present he would be there. According to the newsnaper reports he had not I been credited with all the attendances he had made, but he hoped in future to give satisfaction. (Hear, hear).

div.head: VICE-CHAIRMAN.
div.p: THE VICE-CHAIRMAN.

_ Mr J Whitley thought the honours ought to be dis- tributed. Whilst it was quite right to have their district councillor as chAirman, they ought to vary the appointment of vice-chairman. He therefore proposed that Mr Clarke be vice-chairman. Mr Mason seconded the proposition which was unanimously agreed to. _ .
. - - Mr C ark, tn accepting the position, said he hopei he would not have occasion to occupy the chair.

THE COMIIHTTEES. The following were appointed on the Dal[ding Corn- mittee : Messrs Davenport, Pearson, Clarke, Pemberton, Whitley, Pilling, and Mounfield. The Lighting Committee was elected as follows -- Messrs Pearson, Fairhurst, !Mclntyre, Maspn, Pember- ton and Whitley.

div.head: FLOODED FOOTPATHS.
div.p: FLOODED FOOTPATHS.

Mr Pearson brought lorw—a-rd-Trn—o.tion of which he bad given notice, that the Committee apply to the Local Government Board for powers to prevent rain- water from flowing across the footpaths. Mr Ma on took it that the object of the resolution was to prevent rain-water running from the down-spouts across the footpaths. Be had noticed several footpaths flooded with water, and not only did the footpaths look very unsightly but there was an element sf danger. Mr Pemberton said the Corporations of Warrington and Widnes adopted byelaws to prevent water running from spouts on to the footpath but they were found of inns use. The remedy lay in having the footpath properly paved. The Chairman said it would bo far hotter if stip could be taken to prevent the flooding of foo paths. could b 3 obviated ny the construction of a channel, by means of a pipe under the footpath. Mr Mason said a channel would be dangerous to pedestrians. Mr Pearson pointed out that the water made ruts in the footpaths which were not paved. The resolution was carriel

- - VALUABLE SUOGEITIONS BY MR DAVENPORT. a' Mr Davenport advocated the formation of a sub- committee to consider the following proposals which he submitted :—(1) To peruse the byelaws as to making discretionary alterations. (2) To adopt the use of notice forms to be applied for to the surveyor and returned to him as directed for buildings, &o, in course of erection and at completion. (3) To:enforce the use of saddle blocks for sewer connections which are to be applied for and supplied by the surveyor at a cost to be

arranged. (4) To approach the district councillor as t) the advisability of providing yard and shedding for use of materials and the steam roller accommodation where mcessarv, the same to be under the absolute con- trol of the surveyor. Mr Mason thought thssuggestions very good ones and proposed that a committee consisting of Messrs Daven- port, Pt mberton and Clarke be appointed to cniasider the matters and report to the next meeting.

div.head: Strong Remarks by the Coroner,
div.p: Strong Remarks by the Coroner,

On Monday afternoon, Mr R Dobson, coroner, held the adjourned inquest upon the body of Nitrick Tucker, of Kitchen-street, Liverpool, engineer on the ca. Traf- ford, who was drowned in the Chapel Basin, of the Bridgewater Canal, on Sunday night, the 27th ult. At the firac inquiry evidence was given that the deceased and a companion named O'Hara, a fireman on the Traf- ford wcra drunk, and that about ten o'clock eight or nine men were on the caaal side near where the deceased's body was found talking in quarrelsome tomes. The inquest WB9 adjourned with the object of tracing these men and having a post-nrortew examination made. Superintendent Pearson acted on behalf of the police, and Mr J W Knowles, of Widnes, represented Mr T Whitfield, landlord of the Queen's Hotel. Dr McDougall, who had made a post nortemex amina- tion of the body said there were no marks of violence and the organs were in a healthy condition. In his opinion drowning was the cause of death. Robert Peers, alias Illbinsen said ho went into the Queen's Hotel on Sunday night at a quarter to ten in company with a man named Jones and stayed there until ton o'clock. 0 a leaving, they went near the Duke's Stables, where they were joined by Peter Wake- field, William Price and Richardson. Then a man named Acton came along carrying a stone bottle and accom- panied by two sailors and another man. The bottle would hold about a gallon. Actoa invited them along the road to have a think out of the bottle and they went to English. Row where Acton told Price and Richardson I. leave the company as he was not going to give them a drink. They went away and Peter Wake- field followed them. Acton then said he was going aboard with his friends, and witness then left them. Acton and the three men with him were drunk and Jones was about three parts drunk. No one had a drink out of tire bottle in his prerence. There was no row.—By Mr Knowles .—Witness was not exactly sober. lie was about half drunk. lie had been to, the Albion Vaults.
Another witness said " he should say they were all drunk."

The Coroner, in summing up, said nearly all the in- quiries in Runcorn where a verdict of "found drowned" was returned, could be traced more or less directly to over-indulgence in strong drink. It behoved those en- gaged in the sale of drink to exercise more care in carry log on their trade; in order that they might remove thi reproac:i from the town. The jury returned a verdict of found drowned an added •• we are also of opinion that the publicans the district ought to exercise more dis.cretion in selling drink to sea faring men and others. We also are of opinion that the evidence of some of the witnesses is very unsatisfactory. Some of them were undoubtedly druok and we recommend that they be censured. We believe that both sailors were drunk when they left the hotel..'

NOTES ON UAIVIES AND ATHLETICS.

Cricket. Cheadle Hulme were fortunate in being able to record a victory as the result of their encounter with Warring- ton on Saturday. Three runs was the margin in their favour, the winning hit being made only a few minutes before the call of time. The attendance of spectators was a decided improvement upon that which character- ized the opening match of the season and a capital afternoon's cricket was witnessed.

The Warringtonians batted first, and at the outset nate represented by .1 Callon and B Siloock. G W Rad- ford and Teather were the opposing bowlers and when the home aggreg‘te had reached 13 Callon retired, a bot drive having been caught by C B Taylor.

J Gibbon, who made nis first appearance in the local team, then went to the wickets and several clever hits gained the hearty applause of the spectators. It WI, difficult to deal with the balls sent down by Teather, and when the score stood at 26 Gibbon was bowled. A few minutes later Si!cock shared a similar fate, having placed 10 runs to his credit.
Teather still continued, to work great havoc with the ball, and Dr Smith and P B Hawtin were sent back with successive bails without scoring a single run.

A Thewlis and J W Bibby made a splendid stand and matters began to look brighter for the nome side. Both batsmen succeeded in making boundary strokes, and 2he score steadily rose to 58. A fresh bowler, Redfern, was then tried, and the change bad the desired effect, for Bibby was bowled in the first over, after contribu- ting a claim rues.

The home profesEional continued to bat in fine style, and together with Podmore added 13 runs for the seventh wicket, when he was sent back by Redfern, his innings havieg realized 27. IV H Podmore retired nine runs later, but a vigorous stand by J Briggs and E Gib- son raised the score to 108 berm the last wicket fell, Briggs taking out his bat for 15.

The feature of the Cheadle Hulme innings was the brilliant tatting of Cadman, whose display was marked hy sound hitting associated with an able defence. His 54 was made without a faulty stroke. Teather and Radford passed the home aggregate five minutes from call of time, when Teathcr was bowled and stumps were drawn for the day,

div.head: Redfern was the most successful bowler of the afternoon, taking four wickets at a cost of 23 runs.
div.p: Redfern was the most successful bowler of the after- noon, taking four wickets at a cost of 23 runs.

The second eleven drew with Cheadle Hulrae on the latter team's ground. Batting first the Warringtonians gave a:consistent display and excellent contributions by E E Woods 34, 11 Connor, 18, and W Hind 11 (not out) were chiefly responsible for the respectable total of 128. Woods batted in vigorous style for his 34, and included in his hits were five boundary strokes. A capital innings by A B Rome saved the locals from defeat, and at the Close the Warringtoniaes had the advantage in the drawn game, the Cheaule aggregate realizing 97 for tke Ips ot, nine wickets.

Sankey Wire Mills suffered defeat on Saturday, when they had Weaverham for their opponents. For the winners Rogers knocked up 19, and Blain bowled in fine form taking six wickets at a cost of 12 runs. Burton was •responsible for the capture of five wickets at a cost of 20 runs for the visitors.

Bowling. In connection with the Lancashire and Cheshire Association on Saturday, Wigan and Warrington South met at Tylesley, Wigan winning by 204 to 184 ; at Ash- ton-en-Meraey, Winnington Park beat Pendleton by 210 to 192 ; and at Peocileton, Ldgh Railway defeated Ash- ton-on-Mersey by 246 to 188. Bollinwood faced Leven- shulme at Beaton Mersey, the foriner winning by 214 to 170.

It is just possible, however, that the country, if it is consulted on the subject, may prefer some extension of the board system, which is already an Organized growth, noL only living, but thriving, and with much good 'work to commend it to the Public. Perhaps the most extraordinary feature of this ingenious scheme is that London, though a County, is not to be permitted to entrust its education to its county councils, but the school board system would be placed under the Technical Beard which would carry it on, with the assist- ance of the recently erected borough councils. Why this is to be done is not stated ; but the patent fact that this cours6 would effectually re- °love education beyond the reach of the only pro- gregsive forces known to London may perhaps anilPly the answer.

IN previous articles on A Liberal Policy of this subject it has been Finance. shown that the Govern- rnent have gone entirely wrong in the principles they have adopted as the basis of their finance. they have followed methods which are expensive, Inconvenient, uncertain and inequita'Ae. They have subjected trade, not only to the petty annoy- ances inevitably associated with an extension of customs duties, but to direct loss which shall have the effect of crippling British commerce through- out the world. They have done more, by reviving the obsolete tax on exports they have introduced the thin end of the wedge into one commercial Mem which must produce a cleavage or a rupture in the entire orbit of economies. The coal trade, the shipping trade, and allied businesses will anffer, but not they alone. One of the chief factors which have contributed to the Phenomenal prosperity of Great Britain during It.t„he Victorian era and next only to Free Trade eli, has been the export trade of the country Cietl, constantly glowing in bulk and in value, sa enabled shippers taking out full cargoes to ring back the produce of all the ends of the earth at cheaper rates than they could otherwise, thus enriching the country with numerous articles of value and luxury which would otherwise have been beyond the reach of the great masses of the people. It was pointed out with some force by Mr. JOHN WILS°N during the debate on the coal resolution, that if shippers fail to get a freight both ways the freight is bound to be doubled for such cargo as theY can secure. A vessel running empty has the same cost for working as if she were full. Any decrease in our export trade will therefore have to ba made up by additional charges on the freight carried on the homeward voyage. This bound to raise the prices of imports, Which now include a very large proportion ef the food supply of the country. The coal-tax has therefore in it the germs of groat and widespread mischief.
