The tie„ latest census returns confirm the expecte- th,,"B which have been made, though here and N a surprise is fund. The broad fact that the kanlanufacturing towns are growing rapidly, that the country places are declining,seems to 14t:,,atablished ; while quite a mournful tale is re- ad to some of the villages. Everyone must tp tt`,3t this concentration, as it must be injurious thega health of the community. We know that 4Etilo alwart policemen of the great towns, the Ntaf' arid the soldiers, are mainly drawn from the tilest districts—or, at any rate, that their Tharp, !IPecimens generally come from them. nloude 18, however, a silver lining. to most and we see it in the information

about the metaopolis. The statistics as to ; London have been issued in sections according to the cities and boroughs within its area. This de- monstrates how regular has been the migration from the centre outwards. The City of London, which looms so largely in the eyes of the world, now has a population of only 26,000. It has lost one-third in ten years. Finsbury, Holborn, Mary- lebone and Shoreditch have also declined. The cause which has acted in this matter is the value of the ground for business purposes. It is very cruel to those people who are compelled to live near their work; but it is not without some Com- pensation. It leads many people to distribute themselves who would other wise be herded un- healthily together. The Housing question is so sad that it calls for strong remedies, but there are signs that everywhere the congestion is being re- lieved, despite the growing tendency to accumu- late in cities.

Until quite recently the people of Warrington took very little interest in the education of pupil teachers, and yet the subject is one of first importance in the teaching of the young. If the standard of elementary education is to be raised the teachers must be highly efficient and they can lbest become so by careful training and tuition in their early years. Hence the necessity of gather- ing them into centres during their years A ap- prenticeship and making it possible for them to obtain entrance into the Training Colleges. A most encouraging report of the work which has already been accomplished t the Warrington Centre was presented at the first dis- tribution of prizes held last week. Of the 41 pupils presented for examination in October last, 23 passed in the first class as compared with 4 in the same class a year ago. Such a result is highly creditable to the principal and his staff considering the difficulties which always confront a new institution, especially in a town like Warring- ton where the voluntary system imposes a more rigid economy than in districts where school beards obtain.

A suggestion was made at the meeting that the pupil-teachers' centre should be removed at the earliest possible opportunity to the new Technical Institute. The present premises in Bank.s.r Aet are ill-adapted for the purpose and they do not meet the requirements of Ills Majesty's Inspector. As classes meet in the day-time there should be little difficulty in providing the necessary accommodation at the Technical Institute, which will be used more particularly in the even- ing for technical instruction. The Ray. Morley Stevenson expressed the hope that the Corpora- tion would consider it a great privilege to educate the future teachers of the town, but the question arises what is to be the cost of the privilege ? If the schemeis simply to relieve managers of volun- tary schools from their responsibilities with regard to the education of their pupil teachers at an annual cost to the ratepayers we are afraid it will meet with a great deal of opposition. The rates question is a decidedly thin-skinned and touchy One.

div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT. _— A Provincial Letter.

When Sir Michael Hicks-Beach introduced his Budget and the accompanying proposals he could scarcely have been aware of the hornet's nest he was likely to disturb. But it has to be said for the present Chancellor of the Exchequ-r that when he has made up his mind he is not easily turned from his purpose. He appears to have been particularly careful, during what is regarded, as the "coal tax crisis," to impress upon each of the deputations that waited on him that he had no intention to abandon his proposal to levy an export duty upon coal. It is for politicians to decide whether the proposal implies a departure fr ,m the free trade principles which have been so long upheld by lead- ing statesmen on both sides in the British Parlia- ment. Here one has only to deal with facts. In the House of Commons on Monday midnight the proposal of the Chancellor of the Exchequer was approved by the fairly substantial majority of 10G But this did not end the matter, inasmuch as the ' resolutionlad to be incorporated in a money bill, which in passing through its various stages will give many more opportunities of opposition. But, as if to further complicate matters, Sir Michael Hicks-Beach has made it clear that the Government propose that this shall be a permanent addition to the revenue of the country, in which case the opposition to the tax may be directed in a new channel, with the no; very delighr ful pro-pect of a horough over-hauling of the whole .of tho present system of taxa. ion,

Thus far the coalowners have not been very successful in their efforts to get rid of the proposed tax. Now, if the tax be approved, can one see why they should be:the loudest in their complaints? For it is difficult to believe that the imposition of a shilling per ton upon a relatively small portion of the coal trade of the country will hurt coal-owners generally, who according to Sir Michael Hicks- Beach's figures, made a profit last year of forty- three millions sterling on a capital of 110 millions. Instances, indeed, were not rare last year of collier- ies making anything between 25 and 100 per cent. profit, and although these were admittedly abnor- mal returns, there are many manufacturing and trading concerns that would welcome a dividend of seven per cent., which Sir James Joicey apparently regarded with contempt as the average earning power !of collieries in this country. The miners are, of course, used as the monkey in the fable used the cat's paws, to draw hi chestnuts from the firs; but it was refreshing to find one of the d-legates to thi London conference remarking, on Tuesday that a general stoppage in the British coal trade would prove the opportunity for the Americans and the Germans toobtain a footing in Europe which they could not otherwise acquire. The firm attitude of the Government on the previous night appeared to have a sobering effect on Tu-sday's conference.

Notification of measles does not appear to find favour, as a rule, among medical men. Four out ot the five medical officers of Exeter have reported against it on the following grounds, viz :—the im- possibility of getting a large percentage of the cases notified owing to no m idtcal man being called in, the. large expense neces-iary in procuring ade- quate isolation, the imoo.isibility of the existing sanitary et if dealing with the matter, and lastly, but not leastiprobably in the estimation of these medical officers, the fact that notification alone, when temporarily in 1891. d d nothing to check the spread of the disease. The fifth medical officer was in favour of making !inmate. notifiable, but the City Council eau be trusted, it is thought, to adopt the views of the majority.

Liverpool is one of the places in which the eff-,ct, of the Cockerton iotigtnent has already made itself manifest It has borne fruit there in the shape of a resolution to clo,e the evening continuation classes, abandon manual instruction, and dismiss those pupils who are above the age limit from all the scools, both Board and Voluntary. This looks serious, bat it is regarded as being in strict accor- dance with both the spirit and the letterof the edu- cation Code. In England it may be advisable to let things remain as they are until a system of inter- mediate education is introduced, but the situation is far from beir,g agreeable. In vV ales they appear to have maionged theoe things 'oetter. Secoothry echo ils there are already in opera'ion, and tho:e parents who are desirous of having their children taught simething beyond the, which is provided in the Code are at liberty to send theca to those institutions.

--- Earl Spencer has already pointed out in the House of Lords they, unless Foam action be taken, greet and serious detriment will befall the educa- tion of the country ; but all that the Duke of Devonshire could be induced to say was that, in the Education 8,11 dif this Session, the Government will make such provi,i3n as appears to be r, quisite for maintaining proper instruction in evening con- tinuation classes, and that he had little doubt some means would be found to relieve managers who carry on existing schools and classes, while legisla- tion is pending, !r ,m any personal liability for sur- charges which might otherwise be visited on them. It is certainly ungenerous, to say the least, to en- deavour now to shift the whole of the responsi- bility for what has happened in a number of schools on to the shoulders of the School Boards,and to take shelter behind the plea that the Board of Educa- tion has no responsibility under the Act for the ex-

div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, MAY 10, 1901

penditure of the school funds. Besides,there is the I danger that so large a measure as is now con- templated may fail to be passed this Sassion,owing to the many contentious matters before the House of Commons. It would appear to be much prefer- able, and more safe, to have a short enactment that would legalise the teaching of adults in evening continuation schoo!s,and thus avoid a break of con- tinuity in what is admitteily a most important branch of educational activiv.

Relatively, as shown in the first instalment of the official census returns, London has not grown so rapidly as some of the largest cities and county towns of the provinces; Leeds. Cardiff, or Bristol to wit But the actual increase during the decade is I' more than three hundred thousand, and the total population now excseds four and a half millions ; a number that is simply overwhelming in its vastness But these colossal figures do not convey the whole truth, inasmuch as there are districts in Surrey, Kent, Middlesex.and Essex that are not returned as metropolitan, but have increased enormously in population ; and this is nothing but the over- growth of London. Hudderrfield, Chester and Bath how a decrease, but the explanation in regard to stddersfield probably is that population mostly de- eloped outside the urban area, which is not pir- icularly extensive, and there has long been an xcellent tramway service there. Chester simply does not grow, and almost the same may be said of Exeter, When the full returns are published it will probably be found that Lichfield, Winchester, and Wells remain practically stationary ; and few will regret their being so. For the charm of these cathedral cities is that they are, not bustling and "progressive." To many people there are few great4r pleasures, after being jaded with life in large industrial or commercial centres, than are ob- tained by wandering in the cathedral precincts of a delightful old-world city, watching the birds sail round the tall pinnacles of glorious temples built in a day when England was really a restful land.

It appears from some of the district newspapers that there are not a few places where the local authorities are much disappointed because the Census returns hitherto published do not corres- pond with the local official estimates of the popu- lation, Some consolation for these people may be derived from the circumstance that, as the Registrar-General has point,d out, the returns are revised and subject to modification. At the same time, they will have to be taken as fairly accurate, since, if errors have crept in, it is doubtful whether the revised figures will show any further sub- stantial difference in the population oc the towns already accounted Lr. It is worthy of note that the figures given for 1891 have been corrected so as to apply to the boundaries of enlarged centres as they now exist, and not as they stood last year and previously. There is little doubt that there have been some minor miscalculations which terd to show the desirableness of a more frequent and systematic census, even if the work has to be undertaken and the cost be borne locally. An in- creased population in the metropolitan and sixty- seven county boroughs of England can scarcely fail to suggest many future problems to the serious minch-d amongst us, however, satisfactory the knowledge is in itself.

div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT.]

The Runcorn Volunteer C)rps entertained their South African heroes to a banquet at the Drill Hall on Wednesday night. in right loyal style. The function was of a semi-privets nature, yet not the less hearty and inspiring. The townspeople are to have their turn presently,

A visit to Proisham resulted in my getting atnonget several volunteers belonging to the de- lightful village; and, arnflngst other things, I learnt from them that next Saturday evening the Frod- sham Volunteers will entertain the returned soldiers of their battalion at the Town Hall. There will also be a presentation of watches, and it is also the intention of the Carps to erect e brass plate, inscribed with the names of the special service men in their new Drill Hall.

The Runcorn and Widnes Teachers Association at a recent general meeting stronzlv urged their claims to representation upon educational Com- mittees. It was very reasonably contende 1 that the teachers notwithstanoing the undue stress laid upon the qualifying word elonenta y, was some- what of an authority upon matters educational,and would be a gain rather than oth,Twi.se to such bodies as the Technical Instruction Committee. The Runcorn Urban District Council came in for some considerable criticism, and rightly deserved it. But then the Runcorn controlling body elects its members for particular reasons. For instance it is well to recall the fact that some time ago several members of the Free Library Cminsittee were elected on the Technical Committee for no other reason than the peculiar one illustrated below.

It app,sared that the Free Library Committee and the Technical Committee met on the same night. The former being subsequent to the latter. The members of the Technical Committee were all (more or less), members of the Free Library Com- mittee, but some of che latter were without the pale of the former, and used often to have to wait in the pvsve of the Town Hill until the business of the Technical Committee was metaled and that of the Free Library Committee commence. The sequel showed the,. " this waiting in the pas. age" became a qualification, and eventually the waiting members were co-opted on to the Tech- nical Committee. Clearly then in face of such reasoning the School Teachers claim that represen- tation is not outrageous.

Local education matters are receiving a check, and bath progressive arid moderatioeist candidates are resting upnn their oars,until they are quite able to grasp the effect the New Education Bill will, have upon the Schooli Board. If. as it appears, School Boards will not be affected in respect to their control of the elementary education and voluntary schoals will also be allowed to assist in that elementary education; there will naturally be no change in local feeling. But, should elementary education devolve upon School Boards alone, and the wards of Sir John Garet be realised. that "School Boards be made universal," the aspect of the Case will be consid-qably altered. At present, however, the Bill is nat understood, and until it is all parties will be without a policy, save a problem- atical one.

div.head: FASHIONABLE WEDDING AT RUNCORN. Downes—Taylor.
div.p: FASHIONABLE WEDDING AT RUNCORN. Downes—Taylor.

The neighbourhood of Halton-road Wesleyan Church, Runcorn, and other parts of Runcorn pre- sented a gay and festive appearance with innumer- able flags and festoons of bunting on Tuesday* The cause of this rejoicing was the marriage of Miss Clara Taylor, third and youngest daughter of Mr Samuel Taylor, J.P.. of Rydal Mount, Runcorn, one of the town's most popular and highly respected citizens. The bridegroom was Mr Frank F Downes, eon of Mr Francis Downes, of Vicars Cross, Chester, a well known gentleman of that ancient city, and the linking together of the two families aroused great and widespread interest. Rydal Mount is in close proximity to Halton-road Church, and car- riages were therefore dispensed with. For the occasion Mr Taylor's residence and Belle Vue, the home of his neighbour, Mr J R Frith, were Liao wn into one, and a special pathway to the church, covered with crimson cloth and with a canopy overhead, had been improvised for the passage of the bridal party, and the charming procession was witnessed by hundreds of spectators, the weather being bright and genial. The staircase of the church and the sacred edifice itself were beautified by large palms and other foliage plants and lovely flowers* The rostrum presented a scene of floral beauty and the Communion rails had also been artis- tically treated. Portions of the church had been re- served for the guests who numbered nearly 200,and admission to the remaining seats was by ticket only, and every available space was occupied some time before the time of the ceremony, 2.30, and the tedium of witting was relieved by music rendered by Mr Reginald Johnson on the organ. As the bride entered, leaning on the arm of her father who gave her away, the choir and congregation joined in singing the hymn "The Voice that breathed oe'r Eden, erstwhius the bride and her attendants grouped themselves in brilliant array at tee com- munion rails. The bride was attired in a lovely gown of ivory duchess, satin trimmed with Brussels lace and frills of chiffon and having a lull court train, adorned with bows of orange blo-som and satin, her hrow was encircled by a wreath of orange blossoms from which a flowing veil of Brussels lace fell gracefully. Her only ornament was a diamond and pearl pendant the gift of the bridegroom and she carried an exquisite boncpaet of white roses and lilies of the valley. The brides- maids were Miss Pattie Downes, Meter of the bride- groom and two pretty young maidens—lvy Frith, niece of the bride, and Kathleen Smith, of Chester , —and they wore shimmering yellow Liberty satin I dresses, trimmed wish fischus and yellow chiffon, Miss Downes] had a hat of crinoline straw trimmed with yellow chiffon, and wore a diamond and pearl pendant, the gift of the bridegroom. The little maids had chiffon hats with yellow plumes and wore gold lockets set with diamonds and pearls, the gifts of the bridegroom Each carried a basket of choice yellow roses. There were also in attendance on the bride two handsome and sprightly page boys :—Master Frank Frith, nephew, and Master Geoffry Sheard, of Liverpool, who wore costumes of yellow satin, and cavalier hats with large yellow plumes, and carried crooks, adorned with yellow roses. The beet man was Mr James Carter, of Frodsham. The ceremony was performed by the Rev Alfred Wells, Superintendent Wesleyan Minister, assisted by the Rev J Bourne Jones, Superintendent of Chester Circuit. Before pro- nouncing the benediction Mr Wells delivered a short address in which he offered Mrs Downes their most , sincere congratulations and said they all preyed that II God's blessing might rest upon her.ller unobtrusive- ness and the sweetness of her disposition had en- deared her to all the people,—the Methodists of this place. God had endowed her with one of the richest gifts, the power of song, and she had consecrated it to the service of her Maker and to the people. Sir Downes' was fortunate to win such a bride, and they offered him their congratulatioas. While they were sorry to lose her they rejoiced that in another sphere she might be able to serve God and make Mr Downes life beautiful and blessed.

It is worthy of note that it was the first rear:iage in Runcorn under the new Registration Act, the services of the registrar being dispensed with and Mr Wells acting in that capacity. l hile the necessary formalities were being observed in the vestry, the pretty little bridesmaids and the pages distributed favours to the guests, and the choir and congregation sang the hymn "0 Father, all Creating,' and the organist played the Beidal March from Lohengrin. Then as the bride and bridegroom passed through the churca to:make the exit the organist pealed forth Mendelasohn's noble Wedding March, the entire congregation standing. Subsequently a reception was held at Rydal Mount and continued in the schoolroom, which was delightfully decorated and admirably arranged for the purpose. The guests were received in the hall of Rydal Mount, the bride occupying a position tinder a bell of white azaleas and maiden hair fern, from which depended a well-worn horse shoe, the emblem of good luck. The catering was in the capable hands of the renowned firm of Messrs. Bolland, of Chester, and , was executed in their usual high-class style. The bride's cake was an exceedingly elaborate and ' ornate production of three tiers, each tier suppor- ted by Grecian pillars. The ornamentation was higtLly artistic, and included a shield bearing Mr. Tay'lor'e crest. The cake was surmounted by a handsome Parian vase and bouquet, with silver bullion streamers and a satin banner bearing the monogram of the bride and bridegroon intertwined. Music was supplied by the Enterpean Ladies Orchestra of Birkenhead, the appended programme being submitted :—Programme, Wedding March from" Loliengrin," Wagner ; overture, "Bohemian Girl," Balfe ; valse espagnole "La Zingana," Erichs ; selection, " Tannhauser," Wagner; Wedding March, Mendelssohn ; country dance, pastoral dance, Merrymakers dance, I Nell Gwyn," Z (xerman ; selection," San Toy." S Jones ; pizzicato gavotte; tarantella, " Corsica," Vandervell ; selection, "Pirates of Penzance." Sullivan; Gov kind per- mission of Messrs. Chapel and Co ) ; Mazurka, "Con Amore," Travers; cyardas, " Dame Styrienne," Michaels. During the afternoon the bridal party were photo- graphed and subsequently Mr and Mrs Downes left by special train for Lime-street, to catch the scotch express. on route for Shandon, where the honey- moon is being spent..

The bride's travelling costume was dark helio- trope cloth skirt, with velvet Bolero trimmed with revers of silk and lask ; with hat to match. Hun- dreds of yards of crimson cloth were used for the pathway and for the church and chr.pel stair cases and floors, and this was subsequently distributed to the poor people of the town. ONE MILE FOOTRACE AT WIDNES.-II BARBER V.
J FLYNN.

This footrace over one mile, which has caused so muchexcitement during the last month, took place on the Lawerhouse-lane enclosure on Saturday. Both the contestants are local lads, and the stake was one of £2O Flynn got off his mark well, and after a very tight race, in which he held the lead all the way, won by a few Inche4. Much com- ment was made on the result, as both men finished well at the tape, and it was a very difficult matter to judge which was the winner.

He said that in answer to the advertisement three tenders had been received. The naines and amounts were as follows --Kitchen and store . Mr le Fairclough £329; Mr C W Daven- port, £290 12s; and Mr R W Collin, £BO9 Bath- room and lavatories: Mr Fairclough, £635; Mr Davenport, £562 13s ; Mr Collin. £599. Totals : Mr Fairclough, £964; Mr Collin, £9OB ; Mr Daven- port. £853 ss.—Mr Pilling moved that the tender of Mr Davenport be accepted.—Mr A Jolley seconded and it was carried.—The Chairman (to Mr Owen): They are all within the estimates, are they not ? Mr Owen said the estimate Riven to the Local Government Board was about £670 exclusive:of beating. The heating would not be much more than £5O, so that the tenders were somewhat above the estimate, The heating was now included. He supposed they could proceed with the work forth- with ?—The Chairman : At once. The sooner it is done the better.

THE NEWLY-APPOINTED ENGINEER—A DISAP- POINIMENT. At the meeting of the Gas Committee the Clerk read a - letter which he had received from Mr. Hubert Russell, the newly-appointed gas and water engineer, stating that he dechued the position, the directors of the Gals [Company, by whom he is emplosed, having agreed te increase his salary. The Clerk also read copy of a letter which he bad written to Mr. Russell in reply, which 'letter was approved. The Clerk repotted that he had '(aa instructed by the Office Staff Committee) advertised Itor a gas and water engineer with a salary at the rate of 11E200 per annum, risiog to 4 maximum of £350 per 'annum. It was resolved that the action of the Office Staff Committee be approved and adopted. WA t ER COM3IITIEE. I The report of Mr Bowes (the engineeer pro tern.), for the past month was read, from which it appearel (a) That Messrs T and T Vicars were desirous of having water mains laid along the front of their works, with hydrants, tor use in case of fire ; (1)) That he had made an inspection of the fire beirt•s and that he found them properly fitted with apparatus, but that in several oases the glass in front of the box had been broken and the key stolen ; and (e) That he recommended that a fire engine be provided for the district. It was resolved : that a water mairrbe laid to Mes,rs Vicars' works on the firm undertaking to pay the cost thereof : that a reward of be offered for such evidence as will lead to the conviction of any person or p?rsons breaking the glass lor, in any way damaging, the fire boxes that the question of the provitioa of a fire engine for the district be referred to the Gas Extensions Committee. Government Board, altering the Newton; District Im. • provement Act, MS, whereby the Council may, with the sauctioo of the Local Government Board, borrow for the purposes of their water undertaking the sum of £25,000 in addition to the sum of £6,000 already borrowed. The Local Government Board stated that the order would shortly be submitted to Parliament for confirmation.

(e) That a sewer should be laid in Victoria-roa I this summer, that sewer should be put in Wharf-road before the Tram- ways Co commence operations, and that a new sewer is also required in Mill-lane—the estimated cost of the whole uf the work being £7OO. It was resolved that the Surveyor prepare a plan showitg the wicket gate and its position in Railwi.e -street, area that the same be sent to. the London and North-Western Railway Co with an intimation that the gate is not considered adequate for the protection of the public • that the sewering of Victoria-ioad and Wharf-road be included in the sewage scheme which is bin g prepared by the Surveyor. It was resolved that Messrs Peace and Ellis beinstructed to complete the matter. A litter was read from Me A C Leslie stating that Lord Newton was willing to receive a deputation from the Council to discuss the question of Newton Common. It was resolved that the matter be referred to the Sub-committee (Councillors Collingwood., Evans,Gilmour. Ornaand and Thempson.) THE HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. The report of the Mtdical Officer of Health for the past quarter was read before the meeting of the Highways and Sanitary Commktee. Dr Watkias staled that during the quarter ended 31st March there were registered births. 112 ; deaths, 60—natural increase of population, 52. The birth-rate was equal to an annual rate of 271, and the general death-rate to 152, per 1,000 of the " estimated population." These rates were calculated on the ratio of increase that pertained between 1881 and 1891' They were too high, hut he hoed and Expected by the 30th June to have sufficient facts from the recent census to produce a more correctly approxi- mate estimate of the population for the current half-year. The infantile death-rate was 15.2 per cent., and the deaths of children under five years of age were exactly 45 per cent, of the tetal number of deaths. Twenty. one cases of infectious diseases were notified-5 3 aver- age annual rate. The cases were—diphtheria, 2 ; ery- sipelas, 3 ; scarlet fever 16,ten of these caw s and a case of scarlatina notified on the 31st Decemher,l9oo --eleven cases in in—were removed to the Isolation flotpital. Nine of these patients have returned home, and two remain in hospital—Otis since 15th February. He had made special Enquiries from brother medical officers of heath as te the most relied on, and therefore the most used, disintecting agent; and without a single excep- tion, they declare in favour of sulphur, Doubtless this is efficient ard sufficieat for empty rcoms, but such articles as bedding, blankets, hangings, •do need treatment in a special chamber to secure absolute die. infection. The minutes of the Highways and Sanitary Com. mittee were approved on the proposition of tbe Chair- man.

Hill.—Superintendent Monaghan stated the facts of the case which went to show that Mrs Harper saw the Aid safe in the back kitchen of her thouse on Monday morning In the afternoon she saw Quinn, in company with Mannlon, in an adjoining yard. She missed the skirt on Tuesday morning and reported the matter to the police. Ingniries were instituted, and the police found out that the two prisoners bad been pawning and selling clothes all day. 1 Quinn had pledged the skirt in Mr IS V Morton's pawnshop in St James'-street on Monday afternoon. dannion stood in the do Tway of the shop and afterwards joined Quinn. They met a woman named Glover iR Bridge-street. to whom Mannion sold the pawn-ticket. Both prisoners were arrested, Quinn said, " I took the skirt." and Mannion said '6 I sold the tloket,6"—Bvidence having been called the Chief Constable said the women were posi- tive pests. Mannion had been before the Court 21 times within a very short period for various offences, and the other woman had made 19 appearances. Thy were two very bad and dangerous characters and had been carrying on these Ithefts in confirmation with a gang of woman, who it was hoped would be brought before the Bench at some future date.—Pritoners were sent to goal for three months.

div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
WRETCHED HoIm—NEGLECTFUL FATHER SENT TO
FAISON.

At the Warrington Police Court on Monday, before Mr F Monk; and other magistrates. Thomas and Mary Elizabeth Goulden, Hind-street, were summoned for neglecting four of their children in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suffering and injury to health —Mr Browne, who appeared to prosecute on treba:r of the N S.P.C.C., said the male defendant was a faPtian cutter and a knocker-up, but neglected his work and did not bring in much wages. His wages as a tustian cutter averaged from 10s to 12s weekly, and tie r ceived 7s to 9s for the other work. The chief cause of the case being brought forward was the neglect cf a son aged 18 who was very seriously ill. His case, however, did not directly apply uoder the Act. The de- fendant's house had been visitcd by Mr Frank Aukland, relieving officer, and Inspector Hackett, who found the place in a very neglected condition. husband, wife, and four children slept together in a bed on the door, The children were suffering from tuberculous disease. The whole helms was extremely poorly furnished and there was no If cod. 'nine was no improvement on subs, quent visits, seri it was deemed necessary to call Dr. Bowden in. 'Tne msdical advice was that it would be advisab'e for th • children for a time to be sent to the Werkhouse, viLere they would receive proper attention and nourish- rnent.—Mr Aukland said the house was not fit for a pig to live in. The woman complained to him of her hen-- band's bru'alitv. The cause of the trouble was drink lane idlenees. —lnspector Hackett described the house ard the cendition in which he found the ehildren. Be hid he said scores of similar cases in the town under observation, but generally an improvement followed hie visits. Tie defecdants had gone worse instead of hetter.—Dr Bowden having also given evidence, the charge against the woman was withdrawn and she was called as a witness. She said her husband did not' drink too much ard did not ill-use her.—Detendant said if he was giv en another chance he would do better.—He was sent te gad for a month—Mrs Goulden was then ashrd whether she would consent to the children being taken care of in the Workhouee during the month, and serer some hesitation she refused.--The Chairman said that if she came up agaln the would be sent to gaol fo three months.

div.head: Petition to Sir John Brunner.
div.p: Petition to Sir John Brunner.

The following is a copy of a petition to Sir John Brue.ner, Bart., M.P. Dear Sir,—l am instructed by the Executive Commit. tee of the Beirty for the Reform of School Discipline to express to you ttieir extreme regret at the action taken by the Runcorn, Whiles. and N erthwich District Teachers' ASSOCi&tiCII in sending to you en the 23rd ult. a el, putation to plead ler the abolition of the corporal pcnishmsnt record la iok. The advantages ot the cor- poral punishment book are, when accurately kept, m mifold and important. As one ins-Ance we would cite the following. At the March Meeting of the Billing. hay United District School Board it transwred that H M Inspector. Mr J II Davies, wrote regarding the punish- ment bock of the Billinghay Board Infant School that 'there must be semething radically wrong with an Infant school where 378 recorded cases of corporal punishment occur h- tween 12h November 1900, and 12th February 1001 " On an average attendance of 78 we thus have disclosed the " Caning of babies" to the extent of about ten per cent daily. The only excuse made was that Many of the cases were of a very trivial nature, by which is meant that the little children's bodies were not injured physically. N Jw,we claim as every educationist will admit, that this physical-force government teaches children to appreciate physical force and to do right not of their own desires but through fear of flagellation when la the arena of that artificial restraint and not when on their own responsibility. But as the thief aim of true education is the production of self-governing beings—not beings requiring to be governed by others—corporal punishment is most pernicious to and the very antithesis of education. In Scotland generally there are no punishment books kept in the schools, and it is very seldom that that the curtain is lifted to per- mit of even peeps at these " educational tragedies." According to a recent report in the " Perth Constitu- tional " of the prosecution of a teacher the defendant deponed that there were about 20 per cent, of the chil- dren thrashed at one time for mistakes in a spelling lesson. We know this to he a not uncommon regime in Brith scholls. We respectfully and earnestly petition you to use your great influence to abolish all the multi- farious grades and modes of corporal punishment f rem Briti-h schools, and to substitute the natural and educa- tive methods of discipline. This we do in the interests of education, humanity, and applied Christivity. Onr proposed reforms are extremely feasible in the I bands of competent teachers aa is indisputably evinced by the fact that corporal punishment has been abolished trim tile schools of Prance, Rolland Bi-loaim, Turkey, New York, Chicago, Cleveland, parts of South Atm. trail a , many British schools, including Garnethill Public School, Glasgow, Ackwarth School, Pontefract, Great , Ayton School, York, Newtown School, Waterford, Griffin "ant School. Blackburn, University College Schcol, London, aza. So eminently satisfactory are the results in actual practice that not one of these countries or tr,WEIS has ever reverted to our present-Jay system which is merely a varnished relic of the pristine barbarity and superstition of our forefathers especially of the Tudor period—Eton and other such colleges hav- ing served as the main pipes for the diffusion of that ignorant superstition—flagellation. I have the honour to be,—Yours faithfully, LEWELLYN W WILLIAMS, Hon Secretary, Society for the Reform of School ,

div.head: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.
Review of the Season 1900-1.
By " Ovalist "

It is all over at last ! The season 1900-I—an unusually prolonged one for Warrington—has come to an end though one event _still remains undecided i.e the South-West Lancashire Cup Ciropetition. There is something novel about the Warrington club playing right up to the last day of the football season, and something really remarkable about them being in the final ties for the two cups at once. Those interesting events are dealt with else- where, however, and my purpose here is to review the events of the season just brought to a close. 'there can be no questioning the fact that I the season has been the most successful one War- rington have experienced for many years. They have not won anything, unfortunately, except a little extra fame but the performances of the past eight months will compare favourably with those of any period in the club's more recent history. Warrington possesses a really good team at present with a decided weakness only in one place—at half bacic—and on some days even the halves would take a lot of beating. Moreover it is a young team, with an average age of 24 years, and in great m.msure it is a local team. The players, too, are a decent lot of fellows who work well together and take some pride in the doings of Warrington as a club apart from the financial advantages accru- ing to themselves. This is the right sort of spirit ' and the right sort of team, and when The more apparent defects have been remedied by enterprise and good management Warrington should reach once more the highest pinnacles of football fame. They have been very near such an achievement this year. but the time has evidently not quite come,and we must exercise a little more patience. During the past season there has been a marked absence of

poidhing only two men of any note having been importeu, and those two, Edmondson and Fell, are ! real good 'uns. Welshmen are at a discount just ' now,land Warrington is relying entirely on English talent at present. Most of the men have been available in the pest, but they are young and are only just coming into their best form. One of these G Dickenson, this right centre, is a local youth of nineteen, who bids fair to make one of the best players who ever donned a Warrington jersey. Already he has acquitted himself well in the best company and everybody has perfect confidence in his abilities. The full-back position has been remarkably by .7 Hallam, an ex-three- quarter who has dropped into the right place and now possesses few superiors in Northern Union football. Isherwood has captained the team during the great pert of the season and right well has he acquitted himself both as captain and player, while on the left wing J Fieh has been better than ever as the mainstay of Warringtoe's attack. The retire•cent of J T Bate is a _ _ . _

feature of the se.•;s-OW-I -;ati-not- overlook, for " 6mack " has long been Warrington's crack player, and in the last ten years has led the team to many a great victory. even yet he could hold his own, I believe, if he would only pay the necessary atten- tion to physical fitness, but I fear now we have said goodbye to "Smack "as a footballer. There is still " one of the family playing—R Bate—who has done very good work at the base of the pack, particularly 4uring the cup-ties. Burgess, Duck- worth and Allen can also be relied upon here, but a claQs man is undoubtedly the sine gnat non. Finan- cially Warrington have surpassed all records, and more gate-money has been taken than ever before, the expenses, too,have been heavy,but the business department has been in good hands, and Mr Pem- berton will probably show us a satisfactory balance sheet. Mr Ashton has made an enthusiastic secre- tary and has worked hard in the interests of the club. The committee has been fairly good though its business instincts are none too ante,and the personnel might advantageously be changed a little. Tatra are big developments pending in Rugby football, and Warrington will have to be smart to maintain its position in the forefront of the game. The Northern League was formed on ThurAdav evening and consists of Bradford,Swinton Batle v. Oldham, Salford. Warrington, riuddersfttld, i-falifax. Hull, Runcorn, Broughton Rangers and Hunslet, with power to add to their number. This has tie.•n one of the inevitabilities since the North- Union was formed,the tendency all atom, having been to follow the lead of the Association clubs and have one big premier League. I am glad that Warrington are placed among the " starters," and there snould be an attractive fixture list next

season. Probably Leicester, Durham, West Hartle- pool and South shields will COMA over now. The , big responsibility that this new league places upon' the members of it must not be overlooked. It will need a long purse to cope with the greatly increased expenditure, and a better team than Warrington at present possesses to keep clear of tbe bottom position. The Club will have to be very wide-awake indeed in the future, and energetic enterprising management is more than ever neceesary. I would keit add that nominations for committee and officials muet be placed on the board at the "Golden Lion "before May 10th next, so the., no time must be lost if the best men for the positions are to be secured. Now for facts and ' fieures„ warrington made a good beginning in September ' by winning the opening match at Widnes, and then defeating Salford at Wilderspool and drawing with St Helene—an immediate and clear gain of five points on the previous wit. Then followed successive defeats by Stockport and Broughton Rangers away and Swinton at home, the "Blues " recording a decidedly lucky victory by a try to nothing Thee matters Proceeded on the usual lines, gains and losses about balancing each other. A fine performance was achieved in November againQt Rochdale Hornets, whose path of success was barred by an adverse seem of 21 points at War- rinwtori. Next week Barrow whacked Warrington by 14-5, and the week after the " wire-pullers " went to St. Helene and scored 7-0. The table of results was following the motion of the shuttlecock and consistency was despaired of, A notable match was that eeith Oldham at Warrington, when though W arrington lost by 6 noints they were not dis- graced. No less than four players retired injured, and the Oldham men heti only eleven men to face et the finish. A draw with Barrow, and victories aver efillom,Brieughtonfßangers and Steckport closed the Lancashire League fixtures, Warrington taking iv the sixth ole in the Competition table with a record of la wind, 11 losses, 3 draws, 149 points for, and 126 points against. In the League games Warrington defeated Widnes, Wigan, and Rochdale twice, Salford, St Helens, Stockport, Broughton itangers, efileem and Leigh once, while the draws were with St. Helens, Barrow and Leigh. Swinton, Runcorn, and Oldham, each obtained four points out of Wartington, and single victories at our expense were recorded by Salford. Stockport, Broughton Rangers, Barrow and Millom, Warrington's sudden jump into form with the commencement of the cup-ties is well-remembered. and the progress of the teem to the finals of the , Northern Union Cup,and the South-West Lancashire Cup is too recent, to need dilating upon here. In the ' former Warrington defeated Leeds, Eleckmondwike, Leeds Parish Church, Bradford and Caerieford, Batley defeating them in the final. In the other , cup competition Widnes and St Helens were the victims, a draw being made with Leigh in the final. The Works Competition has been a decided suc- cess again this season, tOrile very good matches having been played. The final resulted in a victory for CroQfield's, who were opposed by Richmond's employes. Much interest was shown in the matches and the proceeds eXeeeded those of previous years. so that local charities will again substantially benefit.

div.head: MAY DAY PROCESSION.
div.p: MAY DAY PROCESSION.
Interesting Event at Warrington.

It was indeed a happy idea when a number of local business men determined that this year,at any rate, the incoming of May should be celebrate/ in smile orzanized manner in Warrington: It is some years since Warrington people made any effort in this direction, but it is now hoped that the May Day procession will become an annual event. Satur- day's processionwas a thoroughly representative ene and there was a concensus of opinion that it reflected great credit upon those responsible for it. The committee which had carried out the arrangements was constituted as follows :—Mr Pretty, Mr Venn, Mr FR Pierpoint, Mr Muskett, Mr T E Pickton, Mr E Isherwood, Mr E Burrows,Mr S Moss,Mr R Spann, Mr F Richardson, VS.; Mr James Newton, and Mr Gordon Roberts.

• The horses and vehicles taking part in the pro- cession assembled on the fair ground, off Winwick- road, at one•o'Clock, and having been placed in order. moved °Toros:lndy at two. The procession was headed by Messrs. Pretty and Moss, who were mounted, and there were two other mounted marshalls—Messrs Pierpoint and Burrows. Messrs Peter i Walker and Son's three horse drays led the vehicles,anu the turnout was a-most creditable one. 'The horses had been well groomed and brightly decorated and some of them wore bonnets—the straw sun bonnets which were so much in vogue for horses in London during the hot weather last year, Then followed a long line of turnouts, over. 100 conveyances and 137 horses being included in the procession. Nothing in the shape of striking originality had been attempted by any of the tradesmen, but probably more will be done in this respect on future occasions. The powerful horses of the London and North Western Railway Company came in for a good deal of admiration, and it was evident that all the horses taking part in the pro- cession are well cared for. The route traversed was as follows :—Wirtwick-road, Winwick-street, Horse- market-street, Market-gate, Bridge-street, Arpley- Station, Wilson-Patten-street, Arpley-street, San- key-street, Buttermarket Street, Irlam-street, Church-street, round the Lamp-post near the church, and back again through Church-street lrlam-street, Scotland-road, Winwick-s'reet, and back on to the Fair Ground. Interspersed among the lurries, drays, &c, were collecting carts for the Warrington Infirmary, and by this means a substantial sum was obtained. Charming weather prevailed, with the result that hundreds of spectators lined the route of the procession. Admirable arrangements had been made by the police, under the direction of Chief In- spector Phillips, and no accident of any kind has been reported. _

The 'following are the names of the owners, tradesmen and others who took past in the procesPion .—Messrs Peter Walker and Son, the Warrington Slate Company, Buekley and Co., E Isherwood, R A. div.p: Itttero to tbe etittor. NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.

Authors of letters intended for publication must In all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor. Matter; intended for publication must be written en one side only of the paper and sent in. if possible, not latter than Thursday. Correspondents are strongly advised to write briefly. A short lett.er has much greater chance of insertion than a long one. We cannot oryl,r ordinary circumstances under- take to return the manuscripts which are not used.
A CORRECTION —ln the letter published in our last issue; and signed Thornas Edmondson, the words " respectlif and recuplrative," should have mid i• restful and recuperative."—ED."Eximiner."
Election Compromises.

Sir,—Kooly allow me ro express my appreciation of Mr Elwin Woods' spirited protest against the hateful compromise, which has been brought about by the two ' political parties, at municipal elections. It is a by no means popular innovatinn among the generality of rate- payers, a good many of whom have found themselves, on occasion, to all practical purposes, dis— franchised as a result of this politicai arrangement. Away with such doubtful deviees to benefit the few ! A few more protests in public like that of Mr Woods at the meeting of the Junior Conservatives will help the compromise to the grave yawning for it, and the obse- quies will be attended by no one with more pleasure than by.—Yours truly, QUEX.

Mr. Edwin Woods—the new Dictator. Sir.—it last the oracle has spoken. After 25 years of sphynx-liks silence Mr Edwin Woods has delivered his eoul. Can you tell me sir, who Mr Edwin Woods is? Hitherto I have not seen much evidence of his activity either in the Conservative cause or anyeither publiebusi- ness. Perhaps he is one of those men who profess to do 'good by stealth" and no doubt since he has become "famous" by his rem trkable oratorical effort he has been in a state of continual "blush," unless he is like those wicked Town Councillors who, recently proved themselves incapable of such an expression of modesty,. I have read Mr VVools's speech more than once and tried to make it into something understandable hut it is so incoherent and so indefinite that I cennot do so. It appears that some evil genius has so beguiled the two political parties that they have gone blindly into tbe " net "and "certain persona" have been compelled to do "certain things" at the bidding of "certain indivi- duals." All this may be perfectly clear as to its mean- ing to the agile intellect of Mr Elwin Woods, but to ordinary individuals it is rather confining. Why does net Mr Woods tell us who are these " certain people" and what are the terrible things they have done ? Does Mr Woods mean that the Conservative mem- bers of the Council are suet' a set of fools that they are utterly incapable of judging for them- selves as to what is right or what as wrong, what is calculated to benefit the town and what may injure it? If be means this then he is casting a slur upon a body of men who are just as clear-headed, as business-like, and as capable as ever Mr Woods was. Mr Woods saye in effect that two or three men in the Coxncil rule the roost and the rest are driven like sheep. Mr Woods ought to support /Rich a position by irrefutable evidence but instead of doing so he has simply made a series of bald assertions as false as they are grotesque. Alder- man Sutton told this newly discovered " Daniel "that it was owing to men of his calibre that the Conservative party had been compelled to make terms with their opponents—terms by the way which have been honcur- ably kept on both sides and leave resulted in better work being done for the town during the past two years than at any previous time since its incorporation. Will Mr Woods fight an election and pay his own expenses 2—Will he even give a few days' bard werk and a good round subscription to help some other Conservative to a seat in the Council? Will hemn fact do anything except grumble and threaten to leave the party if his views are not honoured in the future ? Men like Mr Edwin Woods. who don't appear to know what they are talking about had better hold their peace until they are prepared to prove that the thing they complain about has caused the mischief which they suggest, rather than affirm has resulted. What is Mr Woods after P—Does he want to revive the spirit of bitter political antagonism which was so prevalent on the Council for nearly 20 years that men who to-day are working shoulder to shoulder for the town's welfare would have to revert to a condition of things so unpleasant and so prejulical to the town's best interests that every appointment or preferment was made or coeferred for political rather than muni- cipal services ? If this is his object then lam certain be will not succeed because the commonserne of both parties has compelled the extremists on both sides to recognise the fact that Party Politics and Municipal Government have no essential connection. Now as to the last compromise—has the Conservative Party suffered by it ? I say emphat.cally, ! Has the Liberal Party been injured by It? Again I say, No !" Has any injury been done to the interests of the town? Again I repeat No ! On the contrary the burial of the party " hatchet" has done more to ex- pedite the business of the Council and to remove all ehstacles to that undivided attention to the business of the Corporation which is essential to good government, than anything that has happened for many years past. The main question, however, is this—Shall the pre- sent good feeling which enables the members of the Corporation to give their undivided attention to the , town's affeirs,undisturbed by the excitement and bitter- ness of party conflict be continued, or shall we go back at the bidding of irreapensible individuals like Mr Edwin Woods to the old days of bitterness and party animosity? If the best interests of Warrington are to be the principal consideration of our governing body we must try to maintain the status quo.—Yours, MAXIM.

Enthroning the Bishop. Sir,—Your timely article on the enthroning of the Bishop of London would, lam sure, be welc:Aned by those of your readers win prefer the b^autiful simplicity of the Gospel methods to the ornate and showy develop- ments of modem churchism. I read your remarks with pleasure and, with your kind permission, will now make • few obiervations on the general subj 2Ct.

The enthroning of a Bish-op ! From whence came the ceremony, from above or from below, from heaven or from earth? That it did not come from heaven is proved by the face that we have no revelation on the subject. The New Testament is the Christian's rode meeuPrt,and we searsh its pages in vain for any authority or example for such an exhibition. The founder of Christianity was the lowlies s of men, and spent some twenty years of His brief life on earth as a:wurking man in the vale of Nazareth. And when, on the banks of the Jordan, He commenced His divine ministry there was no throne prepared for Hins,and no crowd of obsequious ecclesiastics to do Him honour. The throne which the Saviour of the world Oeeup'ed was not a material but a spiritual one, and Was only to be found in the hearts of the lowly people,who had been won over to His side by His unspeakable tenderness and love. At the close of His ministry, however, Jesus did receive an elevation and a mitre from the hands ot the religious people of His day. As a reward for all His labour and all His love the Scribes and Pharisees gave Him a Roman cross for His throne,and a crown of thorns for His mitre. Nor did the Apostles have any honours such as the world now delights to shower upon the great and I learned men who, with singular modesty, permit them- selves to be regarded as successors of the humble fisher- men of Galilee. Porsecution and not glorification awaited them wherever they went. Trained in the school of Christ,and thoroughly imbued with His spirit, the Apostles carried out the charge committed to thma under difficulties and hardships of no ordinary kind. And although their mission was marvellously successful their reward was, like their beloved Master's, the easrtyr'e crown. But it may be urged against all this that in the crowning and enthroning of a Bishop men do honour to Christ Himself, inasmuch as the good man is supposed to be His servant. Well, there can be no doub'. that the best way to honour a master is by loving and willing obedience to his expressed commands. But whoa and where did Jesus ever lay it down that He would regard the robing and enthroning of an ecclesiastic at an honour done to Himself ? The scriptures are absolutely Silent On the subject. On the other hand, however, we have abundance of testimony that the Pounder of Christianity never intended that one section of His followers should lord it over their brethren, or be mixed up with the pomps and vanities or the world The following yassages from the New Testament are, I think, sufficient to prove this—" Jesus called them (His disciples) unto Him, and said, ye know that the princes of the Gentiles exercise dominion over them, and they that are great exercise authority upon them. But it shall net be so among you ; but whosoever will be great among you let him be your minis- tor; and whosoever will be chief among you, let him be your servant," (Matt. xx, 25, 26, 27). And again.—" Be ye not called Rabbi ; for one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren. And call no man your father upon the earth ; !for one is your Father, which is in heaven." (Matt. xxiii. 8. 9 ) I cannot believe that the unworldliness and humility a U-. 061 scriptures are anything but a solemn condemnation of the lofty position and titles of the Right Reverend, and most Reverend Fathers in God. But if we are bound to fail in identifying the mitre and the throne with the gospel of Christ we can have no difficulty in tracing them to their proper source. The Balers of the world, Christian as well as heathen, love to gloss their institu• Hens with a religion of some sort. In this country the State !singles out one of the larger sects to carry out itsi idea of a church. And that this sect may perform its various functions satisfactorily the nature and manner cf State worship are clearly defined in a book which cannot be altered without legal authority. " The

div.head: WALKER FOUNTAIN.
div.p: THE WALKER FOUNTAIN.
Presentation of a Silver Model to Sir
Peter Walker.

There was an interesting ceremony in the Town H4ll Warrington,onj Tuesday when a presentation was made to Sir Peter Cerlaw Walker of a silver model of the Walker fountain, which he recently presented to the town in memory of his late grandfather. A special meeting of the Council was held for the purpose and there was a full attendance of members. Sir Peter occupied a seat on the right band of the Mayor during the proceedings. The silver model of the fountain, a description of which • has already been given, was displayed on the Ceemeil table and was greatly admired. The MAYOR oeserved that that was a special meeting of the Cedecil, svcielly summoned for the purpose of making a presentation to Sir Peter Carlaw Walker. (Hear. hear.) When Sir Peter did them the honour to turn on the w ,ter of the foun- tain which the family he represented had en generously presented to the town, and which tssel ad el uet a little to the ornamentation of the Tewn Hall nod surri.und lags and added considerably to the works of interest too few of which,he was sorry to say,the town p -.messed the Council thought it would be a very fitting and proper thing, not simply to be contented with passing a resolution of thanks to Sir Peter Walker and family, but to offer for their acceptance some more permanent memento, not merely of the gift, but ef the many acts of kindly consideration which the town bad received at their hands. (Hear, hear.) The Council thought, after careful consideration, that perhaps the most acceptable Form it could take would be a model in silver of the fountain itself. Be (the Mayor) thought Sir Peter would agree with them that the model reit scted very great credit upon the silversmiths who had brought it into existence—(hear, hear,)—and be hoped Sir Peter would also agree with them that it was a suitable memento of the connection which had existed so long and which had been so friendly on both sides between Sir Peter Walker's family and the Corporation. (Applause). He hoped—io fact he was sure—that Sir Peter would find in it a constant reminder of the warm aporecistion which those acts of generosity had begotten in them, not as members of the Corporation merely, but in their repre- sentative capacity as represen:ing the feelings of those who elected them, and he ventured to hope that it would toe a reminder of the kindly feeling which existed between Sir Peter persoaally and themselves. (El-ear, hear). He would now ask Sir Peter Walker on behalf of the Connell in its representative capacity to accept this memeuto,with the wish that rt any, many years of happy prosperous life would he spared to him and his family, and that they would have him amongst them as often as they would like to see him and that the good feeling which had existed so long might be per- petuated in himself and those who had to follow ohm. (Applause.) Alderman SUTTON, speaking as the" father of the Council," stated that he had known tin present Sir Peter Walker ever since he came into Warrington ;he also knew his father from the time he came into War- rington ; and not only that but be knew the late Mr Peter Walker perhaps as long as any individual in War- rington. He remembered the late Mr Peter Walker from dm first day he earns to Warrington when he (Alderman Sutton) happened to be playing about the brewery. along with the son of the then owner. He had seen the late Mr Peter Walker, the grandfather of the present Sir Peter Walker,working ia his brewer's garb. (Laughter). He had always received the greatest possible kindness from the whole of these three gentle- men. Whenever he bad made any appeal to them for subscriptions for schools or for any institution in War- rington it was very heartily responded to. (Hear, hear). He thought they would begin to know more of the present Sir Peter Walker, and he (Alderrnem Button) thought the longer he knew them the better he would like them and the better they would like him. (Hear, hear and:laughter) He(alderman Sutton) hoped Sir Peter would be amongst them much oftener than hitherto. He hoped Sir Peter would live lung to enjoy the pleasure of looking at the present. (Hear, bear). Ste PETER WALKER, in accepting the gift, paid first of all he should like to take that opportuntty of con- gratulating the Mayor upon the fact that be was the first Mayor of the County Borough of Warrington. At the same time he felt sure that the town m ght be con- gratulated upon having Alderman Roberts asps Mayor. ~(Applause). He (Sir Peter) hoped that the prosperity `which the good old borough had enjoyed might long be continued in its more important position as a County Borough. He could not tell them how much he appreciated this beautiful gift not only for • its intrinsic value, but for the pod feeling which prompted it on the part of the members of the Council towards himself, his father, grandfather and brother. (Applause.) He could assure them of the fact that the gift would be cherished by his famlly. It would be banded down he hoped as an heirloom in the family for generations to come. (Applause.) He was unable to express his feelings as he would like for the handsome gift which had been pre- sented to him that day. At the suggestion of the MAYOR, three cheers were . given for Sir Peter and Lady Walker, Sir PETER WALKER in acknowledging the compliment, remarked that that day happened to be the 47th anni- versary of his birthday. He, therefore, regarded the model as a birthday present, (Applause.) The MAYOR and one or two other members then wished Sir Peter "many hapy returns." The proceedings I then terminated.

div.head: Visit to The!wall Mission Hall.
div.p: Visit to The!wall Mission Hall.

Mr. Naylor's Mission Hall, at Thelwall, after be- ing closed for some little time through the recent epidemic of sickness was re-opened on Sunday, and at tke invitation of Mr $ A Naylor. through Mr Morris, several of the members of S. Janaes' Sunday afternoon meeting for men paid a isit to the mis- son. A meeting was conducted by Mr R A Naylor who gave an excellent address entitled " Right and Wrong." Mr Naylor also spoke very feelingly of two of the children connected with the mission. who died during the epidemic, and at the conclu- sion of his remarks a 'memorial bymm was sung. The service throughout was most interesting and instructive. Afterwards the party adjourned to Cuerden Hall and were shown through the house. Before leaving they were served with refreshments, and each one also received two little books, one en- titled "Here and There" and the other "Seithinys."

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
A Warrington Volunteer Dangerously 111.

We regret to learn that 7171 Private Arthur Richardson, who went to the front with the third contingent of War- rington Volunteers, is lying dangerously ill at Heidel- burg, suffering from enteric fever.
Volunteers all Coming Home.

All the Volunteer service companies attached to the different regiments at the front, Mr Brodrick stated in Parliament on Tuesday evening,are now on the way to Cap-town to embark for home, as also are some hun- dreds of the originally enlisted Imperial Yeomanry, and Lord KiLchener has informed Mr Broderick that he hops shortly to be able to dispense with the services of the remainder of the original Yeomanry force.

div.head: Return of a Newton Volunteer.
div.p: Return of a Newton Volunteer.

Oa S iturday night Mr. Sydney Smith (son of Mrs. Smith, Brookside, Newton), who went out to South Africa With the Suffolk Volunteer Company, returned to Newton, and bis arrival was signalled by a discharge of detonatora. We learn that Mr Smith hss been engaged in the clerical department of Lord Kitchener, He went from College to the war.
The Late Sergeant Owbridge.— Memorial Service at Wargrave.

An in memoriam servlce was held at Wargrave Church on Sunday, as a token of respect to the late Sergeant A 0 wbridge, whose death was recorded last week. The morning was beautifully fine, and there was consequently a large gathering of people. The Earlestown prize band turned out, and headed the local branch of the Loyal Orangemen's Society,of which there was a large muster. Following these were the members of the Mee' Bible Class connected with S. John's Church. Preceding the band, were several members of" G" Company of the South Lancashire Volunteers, in charge of Sergeant Bayley. The proces- sion was a most respectable one, and crowds of people, attracted probably by the music,accompanied it on the way to the church. It was intended to sine a couple of hymns at the residence fMr 0 erbridge in Wargrave road, but owing to the late arrival of the procession this part of the proceedings had to be abandoned. A short stay was, however, made opposite the house whilst the band played the verse of a hymn. On arrival at the church, much difSeulty was experienced ic finding seat- ineaccommodation,in fact s very large number of people wf re unable to obtain admittance, and were conse- quently compelled to hover round the precincts of the church. The members of the 0 xbridge family were present in the church, and the Rev J Carson conducted the service, which included some portions of the burial service. The rev gentleman in the course of his service referred to the duties of a soldier, and to the sacrifices made when he gave up home and life in the service of ' his country. At the clone the organist, Mr E Leyland pl.yed the Dead March in "Saul" the whole congregation respectfully standing. A procession was formed after the service the band playing sacred music on the return home.

div.head: Runcorn 'Volunteers.
div.p: The Runcorn 'Volunteers.

On Sunday morning the Runcorn Volunteers mho have recently returned from the front, attended a thanksgiving service at the Parish Church,accOrnpanied by the membera of the Runcorn detachments of the 2nd V.B.C.R. The Volanteers mustered in strong force at the Drill Hall, under the command of Captain Ashton, and marched via Greenway-road and Bridgewater street to the church, the band leading the way with stirring music. Their progress through the streets was I witnessed by large crowls of people. As the men Bled into the church the organist(Mr F R Boraston)played the National knthem, the congregation meanwhile standing. IThe service opened with the processional hymn "Praise my soul the King of Heaven," and the prayers and lessons were read by the Rev ES Oliver. In the general thanksgiving special mention was made of the safe re- turn of the Runcorn Volunteers. The shortened morn jug prayer was followei by the office for Holy Com- munion, conducted by the Rev Canon Maitland Wood, vicar, who also preached an appronriate sermon from the text Deut., tith chap., 22nd and 23rd verses, " But I must die in this land ; I must not go over Jordan ; but ye shall go over and possess that gosel land. Take heed to yourselves lest ye forget the covenant of the Lord your God." The hymns sung during the service were " Through all the changing scenes of of life " and" Now thank we all our God.

_ At the close the V.Aunteers returned to the Drill Hall, via Church-street, High-street, and Greenway-road. The following were on par Ade : Captain Ashton (in clmmand) Major Harrison,Cap'sin Timmins,Lieutenant Linaker, Sergeant-Instructor Callagan, Colour-Sergeants ' aort and lEhrvev ; Sergeants Holnaes,Rushtnn,Eivrards, Cloper, Lea, Phce iii, Matthews ; and Lance-Sergeants Gittens and Gasket!. Volunteer Service Company : Sergeant Jeacock, Lance-C3rporal Speakman Privates F Platt and L Mack; 30 band and buglers, 70 rank and file. Veterans • Quartermaster-Sergeant Hankinson, Sergeants Woodland, Platt, and Lance-Corpora Buckley.

div.head: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE NEAR RUNCORN.
div.p: ATTEMPTED SUICIDE NEAR RUNCORN.
A Pitiful Case.

Before tbe magistrates at the Runcorn Sessions, last Monday, Margaret Darbyshire, a young girl, of Canon- street, Buncorn,pleaded guilty to attempting to destroy her own life at Sutton, on the Drevious Saturday,.—The evidence adduced disclosed a pitiable condition of affairs Sergeant Bonnett, received information that a girl had been attacked aid thrown inte a pool at Sutton by an unknown man. As the result of inquiries he had a con- versation with Margaret Darbyshire, whom be found at Woodside Farm, Sutton. Prisoner gave her name, she was accosted by a tall however as Margaret Jones, of 129, Horsemarket-street, Warrington, and told a story to the effect that as she ~nviaasn .waanlkdinf for f nneotpltioFnin,g with his wishes the man carried her to a pool and threw her in, Subsequently prisoner went to Woodside Farm and told the same story. At a later period, however, the prisoner told Sergeant Bennett " ill was all lies," and that she had attempted her own life.—Constable John Upton, of Balton, also recounted to the court a very extraordinary story as told to him by the prisoner, is which she re- counted how she had knocked about Lancashire and Cheshire residing at various lodging houses. she also stated she jumped of her own accord into the n pool, but/ it was not deep enougb.—Sergeant Pearson said the girl was a native of Runcorn and her father was present in Court. Trucks on Fire at Lymm Station. The Lymm fire brigade were called to the rail- way station early on Saturday morning, where a portion of a goods train was on fire. Two trucks of cotton were detached and run into a siding where the brigade endeavoured to extinguish the burning cotten, The trucks and cotton were, how- ever, entirely destroyed, the damage being estima- ted at .£5OO. The cotton was en route from Liver- pool to Messrs Whittaker, of the Burst Mills, Ash ton-under-Lv no. •

Parade of Yeomanry at Warburton. The local squadron of " F " (Arley) Troop, " C " Squadron, Coeshire Yeomanry with some tenants' substitutes who live at Altrincham, Lymm, and Dunham Massey.paraded on Saturday afternoon, at Corporal J R Newton's, the Bent Farm. The drill was in plain clothes, dismounted, and with car- bines. Some 15 were present. Sergeant-Alajor Hopper. being unable to come from Northwich, the squadron headquarters. Corporal Newton took com- mand and put the detachment through the manual exercise, some field movements and blank firing.

div.head: LIGHT RAILWAY TO NORTH WIOH. Public Inquiry. OPPOSITION FROM STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: LIGHT RAILWAY TO NORTH WIOH. Public Inquiry. OPPOSITION FROM STOCKTON HEATH.
Scheme Recommended for Approval.

For seven hours on Bator lay last, the Warring- t3n and Northwich Light Railway was under ch.- cussion at a public inquiry held in the Drill hail, North wicb, as to the expediency of granting the application made to the Light Railway Commis- sioners, by Messrs. Brunner, Mond and Company, Mr IH Holden and Mr Joseph Beeketh, for no order to authorise the construction of a light railway from Warrington to Northwich. It was conducted by the Earl of Jersey, G C. 8., and Colonel Boughey, C. 5.1., assisted by Mr Henry Allan Steward, secretary. Mr A Wedderburn, K.C, appeared for the promoters, who were represented by Mr E Milner (Brunner, Mond, and Co.) Mr T Ward, Mr B T Ward, Mr J Newhall, Mr Alleyne Brown (selicitor), and Mr H H Scotter (engineer) ; Public bodies were represented as follows :—Ches- hire County Council, Mr Trevor Lloyd; Warrington Corporation,Mr A A Tobin (instructed by the Town Clerk); 'River Weaver Trustees, Mr Leslie Scott; Northwich Rural Council, Mr A Fletcher; Salt Union, Limited, Mr J L Trafford ; Northwich Urban Council, Mr J Arthur Cowley; Runcorn Rural Council, Mr G F Ashton • Man- chester Ship Canal, Mr Newman; Messrs lireenall.
