Knowles, and others,

div.head: VIE FCHEME &XPLAINED.
div.p: VIE FCHEME &XPLAINED.

Mr Welierbarn olain-d the scheme at considerable length. The project, he said, could be described as the consolidation of two schernei, the first of which had already been before tee Commissioners. Ii November, 1899, application was made to the Light Railway Com- missioners for authority to construct a railwal-; from Warrington to Nortowich, and in May last there was a second application for an extension, swinging round from Northwich and known as the Wes,arro eXten.ion. On June 15th last year the inquiry was held, and there were detects in the draft order, and he understood thee at the suggestion of the Commissioners it was proposed that the matter should not procoed further, but that the two schemes should beconsolidated.ln Novemher last year the present applic glen was made. Counsel proceeded to dese.ribo the railway. Commencing at the terminus of the Warrington Corporation tramways at Stockton Heath swing bridge the light railway would proceed along London-road. On reaching Grappenhell:emad, a line would branch &off and proceed along Grappenhall- road, past Ackers pits and thence to the linutsford- read swing bridge where it would again jirs the Warrington tramways. The light railway would proceed along London-road in Stock- ton Heath, thence through Stratton, Antrobus, Framley. Great Budworth, Marston, Wincharn, and then turning to the west come to Worth- wich, which might be described as the end of the Fast line. Thence it would ptomed north from Northwich to Winnington, Barnton, Whitley, back to Stretton. Warrinetort was an ancient parliamentary borough, with a pooulation of 65,000, and a rateable value of nearly £250,000. It had many Industries and owned its tramways, electric works, waterworks, &c., Stockton Heath was about a mile from Warrington, and was rapidly developing as a suburb of that town. It was an agricultural centre. Northwich WAS an urban district, and had a population of 19,000 with a rateable value of £BO,OOO. It was the centre of the salt trade. Close by were the chemical works of Messrs Brunner, Mond and C ornpany, which were lareer than formerly, because they had recently absorbed th ose of Messrs Bow- man, Tnoinpson and Company. The workplople would be largely helped be the passage of the order. There ' were no trams in Nerthwich, or regular 'buses to the centre of the town, which was a nensiderable distanee from the station. Tee country through wlfch the rail- way would run was agricultural. The east line passed through various places Riving a population of 5,000 to 6,000, and the wester extension gave a population of 4,000. The main line ',seised through various places giving a further population of 3,400 all of whom would be benefited. He thought at Stockton Heath there was a large brewery and Messrs Greenell, Whitley and Company were amongst the fe v activ3 oppon- ents to the passing of the order. As to the necessity of the railway, he stated that Warrington and Nerthwich were only eight miles apart, but there were no means of communication except the high roads, or by a circuitous railway route. At present the agricultural district, Which could eupoly Minehee- ter, Liverpool, and ether centres with its produce, had to travel long distances, at great inconverfienoe and expense. A number of workmen at Northwich had to walk four or five miles. He would call Mr. Milner, one of the directors of Messrs Bru.nner, Mond and Company, who would speak of the immense advantage the line would be to their works. The gauge was to be 4ft Bein andithe estimated cost of the whole line was E 120,000. Dealing with some of the rn ltters which remained un- settled, he said the Weav ir Trettees were objecting,' to two swing bridges over the river so near together, con• tending that this would impede navigation. The Weaver Trustees sail one bridge was all they wanted, and although they did not mind substitution, it must be substitution and not addition. The answer of the pro- moters was that this could not be done under the order. I because the existing bridge WIL4 part of the highway, land they had no power to divert the highway, Us I would be pleased to agree to the diversion of the road if possible, and if the Commissioners were of opinion that there should not be two bridges, then the promoters would have to be content to have a clluse inserted to meet the Weaver Trustees, that they would not open the new bridge unless they got legal pow ers to divert the highway, for which they would ' have to go to the Quarter Sessions, or obtain an Act of Parliament. The only other thing outs.tanding with the Weaver Trustees was the N tton Bridge, regarding which the Trustees said they had Just built it at a great cost, and seeing it would be of such advantage to the promoters they asked for a ren- tal, and he did not think his clients would have any ob- jection to this. With regard to the general evidence. Mr I Ward, managing director of the Salt Union, Mr Holden, and others occupying influential positions, would sup- I port the scheme. The extension line might be described as forced open them by the Parish Councils of Winning- ton, Barnton, Little Leigh, etc. There was no railway oppesition,this having been withdrawn. With regard to the Manchester Ship Canal,the promoters had consented net to make use of their bridges without consent, with the result that they had agreed upon s particular clause with them. Haying done this it was their desire to come to arrangements with the Warrington Corporation who also wished to concur with the promoters. Wit: rineton had been developing their tramways, and they said they might desire to construct the railway them- selves in the Stockton Heath and Latchford Without Districts, and might buy their powers from the pro- moters. The promoters had agreed, if they were content to do this to give up that portion of the line. The difficulty in agreeing Was that they were not sure of their position with the Manchester Ship Canal Company.. . _ -

MI:- Tobin explained that the Warrington Corporation wanted something inserting for their own protection with regard to the Shin Canal, because if they pur- chased the loop line to Latchford they would,so to speak be under the thumb of the Ship Canal, for it would be necessary to cross their bridges. Be suggested the insertion of a clauqp, providing chat if the Corporation of Warrington shoulil exercise their option of construe- ing number one railway, and if any difficuity arose between the Corporation and the Ship Canal Company it should be submitted to the arbitrators of the Board of Trade.

Mr Newman, representing the B%ip Canal Company, said the clause had not been submitted to them and it was premature to mention it now. They were satisfied with the clause agreed upon between the promoters and the company.
ir„ . The Chaman remarked that they could only agree with the law as it now stood.

Mr Lloyd said nething should be done to prejudice the County Council in any action they might take re- specting the extension of the Warrington boundary. Mr Wedderburn remarked that they had done all they could to meet the Corporation, whh might rely upon it they would continue to do so.
Mr Newman said they could not consent to the pro- posal. They certainly VI anted to reserve their rights in the matter. Mr Sutton asked if the promoters Intended to sell the
rights in the railway at Stockton Heath to the Corpora- tion, or was the power given to them to make the railway? _ _

Mr Wedderburn said the promoters would not oppose the Corporation constructieg the line in Stockton Heath if they sought powers to de so. Continuing, Mr Wedderburn a aid there was no opposition from any parish councils, except that of Stockton Heath. That was the place where the brewery of Messrs Greenall, Whitley and Company, was located. Mr Clarke did not think any misunderstanding should be allowed to go unchallenged. Messrs Oreenall's brewery was not in Stockt m Heath. (Hear, hear). Mr Wedderburn, continuing, proceeded Co speak of I the position of the County Council respecting the order. I The two main points of difference between them was with regard to Winnin•fun' bridge And the width of the roads. The County Council desired, that the road should be widened to 27ft. except where the authority said it was not necessary for the promoters to do so. The County Council also urged that the work should be com- pleted in three years instead of five. They farther asked the promoters to provide depi`A at their own expense. The County Council also desired power of parchase, which was a proposal without precedent and to which the promoters strongly objocted. There were also ob. actions from Messrs Grafton, Whitley and Co., who said the roads were narrow, and they alrealy occupied them with drays, &3—(laughter)—and the light railway would interfere with their business. Lie (Mr Wedder- barn) pointed out that there were other industries en- titled to consideration as well as tha of the brewers. Messrs. Oreenall Whitley and Company were large brewers but they had no preicriptive rights to trade. Perhaps the objection arose beckon° they were afraid the trains would not stop at the public houses in the same manner as trained ivories did. (Laughter.) As regarded the Cycle Twirl eg Club, they were ready to give them the Mansfield Clause. The chief land owner against them was Mr T J Down, who lived at Under- cliff o. He objected to an electric tramway running in front of his h lase. Oa the other hand the line was much desired by the poople generally, and there was no question that it would be a great boon to the distriot,and he hoped the district would get it.

AN EIOPERT'S OPINION. Major Philip Carder?, of Mee 4rs Peeece and Cirdew, Westminster, London, said that speaking generally he could reoommend tlaa scheme. He did not think there were many points at which the road could be described as narrow for a single track of lino. Be agreed with the engineer's estimate of the cost.—la answer to Mr Sutton, the witness said the estima'a of £6,500 was too email a sum for ne bridges.

Robert Herbert BeAter said he was a member of the Institute of Mechanical Engineers, Munich, Germany. Be had for rime years past been almost exclusively engaged in light railway work both in this country and abroad. He was the engineer ."lo the present scheme, and produced the plane and estimates. Be was also res- ponsible for the cartoons which bad been prepared, and was thoroughly familar with every detail of the route. He then proceeded at length to describe the route in detail. It would be neceseary, he said, to widen the road in several places, to build a new swing bridge over the Weaver, aud partly to reconstruct B srnton Bridge. In answer to Mr Wedderbuen, he said undoubtedly there ought to be a better means of communication in the district affected. Regarding the financial position of the promoters they were gentlemen of substance. eross-examined by Me Sutton, he attid they were not going to widen the streets in StocktonlEleath to 40 feet unlHiS that obligation was put upon thorn by the Commissionru•s. rho narrowest part of the roadway in this township was 22 feet, Tney proposed to provide ample signals, and agree to any reasonable regulation for dealing with the traffic. As reearded Latcnford Without be understood a clause would be inserted for the protection of the Runcorn Rural Council, in whose districts the roads were. _

Mr G F Ashton said no arrangement bad been made with his Council, nor had any clause been agreed upon. M • &otter, in answer to ;farther questions. said a gre t deal of the goods would WI carried by night. The total weight would vary from 25 to 40 tous, and the train would consist of a motor and two etre. He thought the private owners at Appleton had eaceived much coosidcratiou, and was o! opinion they Would not suffer if ordinary precautions were taken. Tatty would only us- electric power. He was not aware that the vicar of S:ockt m Heath strunr,ly opposed the ache on the ground ofdanger to the school eipliren. The most modern appliances for safety would be utilind.

A CRTICIAL STAGE. Mr Sutton asked if it was not the • fact that there was nothing in th ) or ler giving the promoters power to pur- chase land so as to secure a uniform minim im width of 27ft. as required by the County Council. HI suggested that on 81 miles of roa I that ml ‘imuna was not reached, and there was no fguarantee that if the order was granted the promoters would be aole, PV 'n if they were , willing, to acq tire the necessary land at every part. Mr Lloyd, tor the Cheshire C mots, Council, made the same objection. 'Erie scheme last y4a,r, he said, had broken down on a similar groued. At this point inquiry was al mrnsel for lunch. For the promoters Mr Weddernurn eventually agreed to include in the order what is known as the " Orms- kirk clause," whereby the whole of the roads would be widened to 271 t except in c ts'es where it was not con Sidered nec.ssary. Mr Lloyd accep'ed that clause if it would be taken to include the bridges as well as the roads.

Lord Jersey said the Cimmissioners were agreed that the roads should be so widen-Abu he did not think the promoters should be called upon to bear the whole cost of rebuilding the bridges even to in ike them as wide as the roads. On this understanding is good deal of the opposition was withdrawn. MR. CLARKE' ASKS A NUMBER OF QUESTIONS. Mr Clarke put sOrte p 0 nted questions Co the engineer. IMr Scotter. Witness said that the promoters charges would be less than those of railway companies. He was 1 not aware that the proposed charges were higher than those of the LIsN. W. Railway Co. Light railway charges were, as a rule. less than ordinary railway charges. The list of charges would be scheduled and every informa- tion given. Witness remembered speaking on the sub- ject of the light railway at Stockton Heath the other day. He did not give a lecture ; it was a simple state- ment he had been ask 1(1 to mike by several residents as to the objects of the railway. The loop line at Stockton ^ath was to be made from the Mulberry Tree to Latchford where it would again connect the Warrington tramways. Every light railway in an urban district was more or less a tramway for the simple reason that they ' carried more passengers in the urban districts than goods and more goods in the country than passengers. It would be a light railway at Stockton Heath of the nature of a tramway. On an ordinary railway one was allowed 100 Os., of luggage as a third-class passenger ; on a light rai,way only 2811:19. There would be more passen- ger trafß at Soockton Heath than luggage tratll3. The provision of a waiting room was awaiting the suggestion of the lolal authority who had not agreed about the matter. He had offered to consider any position, but he could not get a suggestion. It was not his duty to find out where the waiting room should be. Hs knew the stone delph at Appleton. If a train started there and one brake refused to act he did not agree that there would be nothing to prevent the car from running into the Ship Canal. (Laughter.) The other brake would act. If a waggon from the Cheshire Linos was offered if would notlhe acc,pted on their line during the day. They had not come to an agreement to unload at the Canal side at Stockton Heath but it was probable they would. They would deliver goods in Stockton Heath if the Parish Council would suggest facilities. He did not agree 1 that Stockton Heath would derive no benefit from the use of their roads by the promoters.

The promoters would not touch his (Mr Davenport's) property in that street. They would take about half the canal yard and leave the steps where they were. Mitchael-streec dipped down. They would not alter the span of the bridge and the road would not be materially altered. The bend in the middle of the bridge would be taken out by the substi- tution of girders. They were going to substitute an Iron-girder bridge. The alteration could not be more than an inch and a half or two inches in the middle of the bri ige ; perhaps three inches. People told me that I looked like a walking corpse. I had pains in my legs, and could hardly walk about at times, I was so weak.
